speechtext:
BUSINESS	OF	THE	HOUSERight	Hon. L.	S.	St.	Laurent	(PrimeMinister): Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the house that the government has now been officially	informed	of	the	passage	by	the
United Kingdom parliament on May 31 of the amendment to the British North America Act respecting old age security.
I am sure that hon. members in all parts of the house will share in the satisfaction which I feel at this evidence of the spirit of harmony and	co-operation which	has
marked the joint efforts of the federal government and the various provincial governments in reaching agreement in respect of this important matter. I am sure we would all wish likewise to express appreciation on behalf of the people of Canada, and particularly on behalf of the aged citizens of our country, of the prompt way in which the amendment was enacted by the United Kingdom parliament.
The house will naturally be interested to know the steps which the government intends to take, now that we have the constitutional authority to' implement the proposals made a year ago this month by the parliamentary committee on old age security and offered by the government to the provinces at our conference with them of last December. On February 5, of this year, in reply to a question put to me by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I stated as follows, as reported at page 72 of Hansard:
... it is and will be the policy of the government to avoid any possible delay when agreement has been reached to have that agreement implemented.
In conformity with that statement of the government's position, I wish to state at this time that it is proposed to introduce legislation at an early day to enable the government to make agreements with the provinces to provide old age security to persons in need between the ages of sixty-five and seventy, and to provide authority for the registration of persons over the age of seventy
for the universal old age pensions. That legislation would probably also at the same time provide for the continuance of federal assistance in the payment of pensions to the blind.
The government wishes to be in a position to commence payment of the universal pension beginning with the month of January, 1952, and we wish also to have our legislation respecting the age group sixty-five to sixty-nine ready for implementation effective in January, 1952, in any of those provinces which will have signed agreement with the federal government for that purpose.
The administrative plans for the application of this new old age security program are already going forward. Registration forms with respect to the universal pensions plan are being prepared, and it is proposed to have the necessary supplies of these forms printed within the next few weeks. A small amount of additional staff will very shortly be recruited to deal with applications for the universal pensions which will be administered by the federal authorities.
Arrangements are now being discussed with the various provincial governments to take from their present old age pensions records the information which will be required to pay the universal pension after January 1, 1952, to the approximately 300,000 persons now receiving old age pensions under the previous legislation. For these persons, no additional applications for the universal pension will be required.
The government wishes to be in a position to commence, as soon as possible after July 1, registration of the others-probably some 400,000 persons-seventy years of age and over who are not at present receiving old age pensions. The Department of National Health and Welfare plans, in the six months between July 1 of this year and January 1, 1952, to deal with these applications through the present family allowance offices with the small additions to staff which are contemplated, and to have their records in shape to enable payments to be made in the first month of the new calendar year.
I am sure that all hon. members who recall the initial registration of a much larger number of cases for family allowances in 1945 will share the government's confidence that the same administrative organization, which is now in the process of being adapted to the requirements of the universal old

Old Age Pensions
age pensions plan, will be able to deal with this new problem in an efficient and expeditious manner. These administrative arrangements are, as I say, already being planned with the aim of pressing them forward as rapidly as possible, and they will be pressed forward as soon as the necessary legislative authority is given to the department to carry out the registration for this purpose.
So far as the legislation to provide for the universal contributory old age pension is concerned, the government has come to the conclusion that, in the light of the heavy load of work already before parliament at this present session, it would not be appropriate to ask parliament to deal with this new and important legislation during the next few weeks. Hon. members are fully aware of the heavy load of work which lies ahead of us, and of the necessity we shall shortly face of holding meetings in the mornings, afternoons and evenings in order to deal with the main estimates now before the house and the other items in the government's legislative program already before parliament, as well as old age security assistance and one or two other urgent matters. .
If the universal contributory old age pension measure were the only legislative proposal which would remain for consideration, the government would be disposed to ask parliament to continue to sit in July until it had been enacted, in the hope that it would not be necessary for parliament to meet again in the present calendar year. But that is not the situation. In addition to the universal old age pensions legislation, there are a number of important measures under consideration, some of which arise out of the report of the royal commission on transportation. In that regard it is the intention of the government to recommend to parliament the implementation of the recommendations of the royal commission to the fullest practicable extent, and that will require many amendments to the present Railway Act. This amending bill will be a very important legislative proposal, and one which should receive the most careful consideration by parliament because of its long term effect on the Canadian economy. It is intended to recommend that the bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and that the committee provide an opportunity for representations as to how the proposed amendments might be expected to affect certain interests and localities. We feel that these proposed amendments should be before the public for study and discussion some reasonable time before they are finally dealt with by parliament.

The government in the course of the next few weeks will also have to give consideration to the recommendations of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences. This requires some time for careful study by the government, by members of parliament and by the public, though it does not seem unlikely that some legislative provision should be made before the end of this year.
There are a number of other legislative proposals to which the government has been giving thought. Some of these, like the revision of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, have had to be postponed more than once. It is intended to introduce that legislation and to have it referred to the public accounts committee, where it can be fully explained in all its details. That is the act which provides the standard for the control by parliament over the expenditure of public fund's, and we think it is one that is deserving of careful consideration.
In view of all these considerations, the government has come to the conclusion that it would be preferable to make an effort to complete the work now before the house, to conclude the present session as soon as is consistent with the proper dispatch of that business and to adjourn until the beginning of October, with the proviso that we can meet earlier if circumstances make an earlier meeting necessary. If an earlier meeting is not required by unforeseen circumstances, the government would recommend the prorogation of the present session when we meet in October and the immediate commencement of the new session. There would be plenty of public business-mainly legislative-to require a full session, and we would propose to have the session devoted exclusively to government measures, in the hope of overtaking all important arrears and starting with a clean slate in the regular session of 1952.
With respect to old age security, the reason for proceeding with the old age assistance measure in the immediate future is, of course, that it is the part of the old age security program which involves joint action with the provincial governments and we feel that the provincial authorities should know as soon as possible the precise legal basis for the proposed agreements in order to make their own legislative and administrative plans in the light of that knowledge. Of course it is intended' that the old age assistance legislation will come into effect at the same time as the universal pensions.
So far as the universal pensions are concerned, once authority has been given by

parliament for the necessary registration, it will not make the slightest difference to the public whether the main legislation is enacted in July or October. The government believes more careful consideration is likely to be given to this very important measure if it is held over, and holding it over will not make any difference as to the date on which it will come into force. That in either case will be the earliest date which we consider administratively feasible on the advice of our experts in that field, that is to say, January, 1952. That from the very beginning has been the earliest date on which it was considered that it would be feasible to get this new machine rolling, and that information was given to the provincial governments at the dominion-provincial conference of last December.
Moreover, as hon. members know, the universal pensions are to have right from the start a contributory basis. Now, we have not yet completed consideration of the normal budgetary program of the current year, and the government believes it would be an advantage to have a few months to observe the effects of the recent changes in the tax structure before reaching a final decision on all the precise details of the contributory system to be recommended to parliament.
It will be recalled that the joint committee made no precise recommendations on that point, because it was recognized that it was the inescapable responsibility of the government. We want to be as sure as we can that we are making the right proposals for a plan which is going to affect, far into the future, the provision for old age security of the whole Canadian population.
The government intends to place on the order paper with all reasonable dispatch the proposals required to be dealt with by parliament to give effect, if parliament sees fit to do so, to this program I have just announced.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that
all hon. members will join in the sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) as to our appreciation of the speed and courtesy with which the parliament at Westminster has dealt with the request put forward for an appropriate amendment to the British North America Act. Undoubtedly they have co-operated in every way to make it possible to proceed with this extremely important legislation which the people of Canada have been seeking for some time.
The Prime Minister has indicated that it is the hope of the government that this legislation shall become law in time to make it possible to begin these payments by January,
Old Age Pensions
1952. In doing so he has outlined some of the extensive preliminary steps which must be taken to that end. He has indicated the necessity that a period be devoted to registration of those who would be entitled to the universal old age pension to be provided under this new amendment. He has also pointed out that a large number of administrative details must be carefully examined and worked out as between the dominion government and the provincial governments so that this may be done to the satisfaction of the Canadian people generally.
I am not able to agree, however, with the Prime Minister in his statement that it will be just as satisfactory if this bill is dealt with in October. I do not believe that we should leave this house until we have passed the Old Age Pensions Act and made it law. There are very strong reasons why this legislation should be dealt with before we leave this house. The Prime Minister himself suggested a reason why there is a difference between July and October. He pointed out that it was the desire of the dominion government to be ready to make payments in January, 1952, in all those provinces where agreements had already been reached in regard to this measure and the payments under it. I think with that statement all hon. members will be in agreement. But from the very fact that the Prime Minister introduces the qualification that the payment would be made in those provinces where agreements had been reached, it is quite clear that in the mind of the Prime Minister the possibility was contemplated that some of the provinces might not yet have been able to take the necessary preliminary steps to make that practicable and possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house share the appreciation that was expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) to the parliament at Westminster for having so expeditiously dealt with the constitutional amendment required to make old age pensions universally effective in Canada. I am very happy indeed that the Prime Minister and the government are determined that this legislation shall come into effect on January 1, 1952. It is a matter of very great pleasure to the members of this group, because of the interest we have always taken in this question of old age pensions. My predecessor, the late J. S. Woodsworth, member for Winnipeg North Centre, in 1926 was largely responsible for the introduction of the first old age pension bill. Consequently it is a matter of much satisfaction to us that this legislation has now reached the stage where the senior citizens of this country who have attained the age of seventy may look forward to a pension without a means test as of January 1 of next year. I believe that is in the interests of thrift in this country, because persons who had saved a little something to provide for their old age were penalized because they had made those savings. I am very happy about the changes foreshadowed.
I am glad to note, too, that the Prime Minister and the government are going to introduce the necessary legislation to bring into effect a new allowance for those between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine. I was hopeful that the income test which was recommended by the committee last year would be more generous than the present means test. When the bill is before us, that matter will receive considerable attention. I agree with the Prime Minister that this legislation concerning the sixty-five to sixty-nine age group should be introduced now, so that the provinces may call their legislatures together to make any necessary provisions for carrying out their part of the particular measure.
I cannot say that I agree with the leader of the opposition that there is really any particular reason why the old age pension legislation concerning those of seventy and over should be introduced at this session. The

Old Age Pensions
dominion has assumed the over-all responsibility in that' regard, and so long as the legislation is passed by this government and all the necessary preparations are made to enable it to come into effect on January 1, 1952, I am not particular whether the legislation is passed in July or some months subsequently.
With regard to the proposed autumn session of parliament, that is a responsibility that the government must assume. Apparently the government has quite a long list of legislation. I discussed it with my colleagues this morning, and they believe that this legislation, which the Prime Minister was good enough to outline to me, warrants the calling of a session in the autumn.
The experience we have had over the last several years, particularly since the beginning of the war, clearly indicates that membership in this House of Commons can no longer be regarded as something in the nature of a sideline to a particular profession or business. Membership in the House of Commons today is a full-time position, and members must devote their entire time, sooner or later, to the business of the country. May I just add the thought that I believe our sessions should be on an annual basis. I do not like this business of having a session in a given year, and then coming back and having another session later in the same year. I believe we should have one session during a period of twelve months. The time of sitting should be more or less determined early in the sessional year. I feel sorry sometimes for the members of the government, who are undergoing a tremendous strain, because in the very nature of things a member must be experienced and therefore not in the prime of youth or early manhood. I think it is in the interests of the country and of the government and the people of the country that there shall be a summer recess. Sitting as we did during the war in July and August taxed the health of the youngest and most robust members of this house. Personally I think the house should consider what other houses of parliament have considered-an annual session with a summer recess, so that we may know exactly how to make our plans, and so that we may understand the responsibilities we are assuming when we accept membership in the House of Commons or seek the support of our constituents to send us to the House of Commons.
We are indeed very happy that the improved old age pension legislation is to be introduced and will come into effect. The government must decide when it is to be
introduced, but to know that it is to be intro- ' duced and is to come into effect on the first of January, 1952, is a matter of great satisfaction to the members of this group.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is also a matter of great satisfaction to us that the parliament at Westminster dealt so expeditiously with our request for amendment of the constitution to make it possible for the government to pay universal old age pensions. We also want to congratulate the government on the speed with which they have started the wheels in motion to get ready for the payment of such pensions.
I think that is a matter of great satisfaction to everyone in this house.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has outlined the program of legislation that is to be dealt with by the house some time this year. I agree that we should not try to push through the summer in an effort to get that legislation completed and made law. I do not see that we could deal properly or carefully with such a program if we were to sit morning, noon and night-as I suppose we shall have to do shortly-through July and August.
My estimate is it would require all the intervening time from now until the end of August to deal with that program as it should be dealt with. For that reason I feel that the government is perfectly justified in asking us to come back this autumn to deal with the program outlined by the Prime Minister. I cannot agree at all with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that the old age pension legislation should be passed and made law before the house prorogues. I see no particular reason at all why that is necessary. In fact I see some good reasons, especially concerning the financial aspects of the proposal, why the measure should not be dealt with until we have an ample opportunity to study the taxation measures that may be necessary to raise these funds.
I cannot see a chance of giving careful consideration to the financial aspects of the old age pension legislation if we are to sit morning, noon and night and at the same time try to get committee work finished. It just cannot be done, and it is an impractical suggestion to say that it should be done before we prorogue. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that we can no longer consider membership in this house as a sideline. I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that there are a good many members who have to come from great distances. They cannot get back to their homes to look after their businesses more than once in a session. We must always keep that consideration in our minds. In view

of the fact that some members come long distances and have to remain in Ottawa for a long period of time, it seems to me we have to alter our whole attitude towards the sittings of the house.
I cannot quite agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that we might consider holding one session a year and specify the time. May I make the suggestion to the Prime Minister that he consider the possibility of beginning the session late in the fall, having a Christmas adjournment, and then coming back possibly around the middle of January and continuing until we finish? That might be the best way out of the situation. In the unusual circumstances in which we find ourselves today it is not unreasonable for the government to consider trying to catch up with the backlog of legislation and calling a special session so to do.

Mr. Speaker, when the resolution preliminary to this bill was before the house and, I think, in his budget speech as well, the minister explained that the tariff items dealt with in the bill were not of a very vital nature and that most of the important tariff discussions had taken place at Torquay and would be reported in due course. I therefore have no intention of dwelling on the discussion which took place at the resolution stage when various details were brought to the attention of the minister's representative. Neither have I any intention of going at length into the Torquay discussions because those are still before the banking and commerce committee and no doubt will be debated when the report of the committee comes back to the house. There are just one or two matters closely related to Torquay that I wish to bring to the attention of the house briefly.
I think it is generally conceded that there was a good deal of disappointment at the results at Torquay, perhaps with the one exception of the results achieved between the United States and ourselves. It was natural that there should be some discussion, as there was, with regard to the question of preferences. After all, what is happening now is that our trade with the United States has been increasing and that with the commonwealth has been decreasing. There was discussion, and there will be further discussion as to the basic question of the direction of our trade. In that connection I wish to read a brief extract from what was said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) on the debate on Torquay on May 21, because I think it is worthy of being put on the record here in this connection. Speaking on our trade position, and particularly our trade position, with the United States, he said this, as reported at page 3225 of Hansard:
We have every reason to welcome the extension and expansion of trade with the United States . . .
By all means, let us seek the expansion of our trade with the United States; but let us remember

that this country is set up for trading with the United Kingdom and the commonwealth. That was not done with any thought of placing barriers between the United States and Canada. Our ties of blood, our ties of friendship and our ties of history are too close for the effective erection of barriers between the peoples of the United1 States and Canada, who know each other better than the peoples of any other two nations in the whole world.
Then the leader of the opposition went on to point out the rather striking figures of the increased trade with the United States, and to what a large extent this trade depended on the present emergency and the defence program. He also drew special attention to the decreased trade with the United Kingdom and went on to suggest, pursuant to a suggestion made by a conference of businessmen recently, that there should be a conference of the nations of the commonwealth-
... to seek every possible means of extending trade and removing any barriers which still hinder the extension of trade and of contact of every kind within this great fellowship.
That last quotation is from page 3227 of Hansard.
I just wish to make one other point, Mr. Speaker. This question of preferences is of course part of the question of trying to have our trade as far spread as possible. At the present time we are enjoying record trade with the United States, but it is not possible to dismiss from our minds entirely such names as Hawley-Smoot and Fordney-McCumber. We cannot forget the fact that to a certain extent we are competitive with the United States. It was, no doubt, partly with that in mind that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) pursued the question of preferences which has such special importance to certain producers both on the Pacific and on the Atlantic coasts. In the course of doing so, he got into a discussion with the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) who is also the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the minister made one of those remarks of his which enliven, although they do not enlighten, the proceedings of this house. In answer to a complaint by Mr. Green to the following effect, as reported at page 3253 of Hansard:
I am not too sure that this government would not do away with the preferences entirely if they felt they could get away with it as far as the public were concerned,
the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
Who would stop us? Don't take yourself too seriously. If we wanted to get away with it, who wouldi stop us?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is my hon. friend quoting from his leader's remarks?

No, I am
quoting from Hansard; I hope I copied it
Customs Tariff
correctly. I will quote them now from Hansard direct.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That was pretty well threshed out at Montreal.

Just to make sure as to the correctness-I certainly would not wish to misquote the minister; and I think that he will find that I am quoting correctly- reading from page 3253 of Hansard we find the following:

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Who would stop us? Don't take yourself too seriously. If we wanted to get away with it who would stop us?
Is that the same as I read before?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

We are both correct. That is the important thing. We try to be accurate when we are quoting the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) especially.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is a great political issue. I would thresh it as long as I could, if I were you.

The things the minister says are interesting and we like to quote them. Of course, there is no need of going at any length over the other ground which the minister and I have traversed. We are accustomed in this house to the fact that the minister does not take us as seriously as we should like to be taken. We are accustomed to the fact that the minister is an authoritarian and we do not expect very much. I think I cleared that word with him previously. It is not an offensive word, I believe. This time I think the minister has gone a little further. Let me read again what the minister said. Let me be sure I am right. This is what he said:
Who would stop us? If we wanted to get away with it who would stop us?
That reply was made in answer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) who was saying that the government thought they could get away with it as far as the public was concerned. The only point I wish to make is that it is difficult to discuss these matters, which are of some importance, when we find that the minister makes a retort of that kind, which is not taking the discussion seriously, and which underlines the thing which he seems to be so anxious to say from time to time; not only to say but to repeat and to emphasize, namely, that he thinks this house is not worthy of any great consideration -indeed of very little consideration.
The only thing I want to add to that is that some day, I do not know when, I do not

Customs Tariff
say one year, five years, ten years, but some day, the public is going to wake up to the fact that it is interested in this parliament. After all, it is all they have, as the man said about his wife, "a poor thing, but mine own". This parliament is what the public sent down here, and at the present time some of us say that they have selected a rather queer one. But it is a very satisfactory one to the minister. He can have his supporters say "Good old C.D." to everything that he says, and even say "Good old C.D." to this. It may be that at the moment the public will take very little interest in it but I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it would be better if the minister would take us seriously. This parliament is composed of serious people, and naturally we should be taken seriously. I suggest to the minister that while this is great fun, while it is grand as long as it lasts, some day the people may wake up to the fact that when he is disregarding and making little of this house he is in fact making little of the Canadian people. There is no doubt that that inference has been left because in the little exchange that I have just read the minister has made it perfectly clear that along with the members of parliament he classes the people who elect the members of parliament, and they are to be set at nought.
As I said at the outset, I think the details connected with this measure can be discussed in committee. At the moment I have no need to add anything more.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief in my remarks on preferential tariff because I am anxious to get away to the veterans affairs committee. However, I do want to keep the record straight in connection with some statements made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance.
I am sure he made the statement in good faith, because I know he is sincere in his advocacy of a few packing concerns who manufacture margarine as I am sincere in trying to support the interests of the dairy farmers. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance gave a list of oils that came under preferential tariff, as reported at page 3122 of Hansard of May 17. Actually I am sure it is only a partial list, and I want the hon. member to look it up. I am not disputing the figures that he gave, and I am not disputing that he gave them in all sincerity. But, Mr. Speaker, in order that the record may be clear to the people of Canada, particularly to those whom I am sure the parliamentary assistant is attempting to assist by enabling them to secure a cheap substitute for a pure food such as butter,

may I say that he has not taken into account the fact that these oils are imported free of duty. I repeat, they are imported free of duty. The remarks of the parliamentary assistant did not give us that information. They were imported free of duty, held in storage, and some months later, instead of their being beneficial to the consuming public, as he claims, the price of margarine was increased 10 cents a pound, margarine made out of these oils which were imported free of duty. That was not to the benefit of the consuming public but to the benefit of Canada Packers, and some four or five other concerns.
As I stated, I have no quarrel with the figures he gave, but I hope the parliamentary assistant takes into account this fact. No doubt because of the excessive amount of work that he has to do, he has not been able to assimilate the knowledge which would be beneficial to the consuming public, but I admit it has been to the benefit of the packing concerns. The bulk of the coconut oil now being used in increasing quantities in the manufacture of margarine is processed in Canada from copra or coconut meat, and this product is brought into Canada under a tariff item. I want the parliamentary assistant to know this, because apparently his assistants have not brought it to his attention, probably because they are understaffed or overstaffed in the ivory tower. It comes in duty free under item 113a under both the British preferential tariff and the most-favoured-nation tariff. The figures quoted by the parliamentary assistant, as they appear at page 3122 of Hansard, do not show that.
We had a gentleman in the city of Vancouver, which happens to be the largest city in our province, who made an immense fortune. Incidentally, the city of Vancouver is just across Burrard inlet from the city of Vancouver North from which my good colleague comes. As I said, this gentleman made an immense fortune from importing copra or broken coconut meat which was processed to make margarine to sell at an increase in cost of 10 cents a pound after it had been brought in duty free during the period when butter was short.
The parliamentary assistant did not bring that information to the notice of the people of Canada through the medium of Hansard, although he was very careful to note other things. Peanut oil in substantial quantities is now being used in margarine, and that comes in from British preference countries under tariff item-and again I hope some of the assistants to the parliamentary assistant will look up this item in their spare time. I refer to item 276a (i), free of duty. Mark

Customs Tariff
that, Mr. Speaker. This also applies to tariff item No. 276c, which covers coconut oil, crude, but imported to be refined for edible purposes.
I know that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance did not want to mislead the public, but these facts were not put on the record. The figures that he quoted on May 17, and which appear in Hansard, are misleading. They do not state that this preference was used to increase the excess profits of Canada Packers and their few associates to the detriment of the consuming public who buy a cheap substitute for an edible food like butter. They do not tell the story at all. If you remember, Mr. Speaker, much ado was made about whether the oils were edible or not edible. For instance, coconut oil, crude, when imported to be refined for edible purposes comes in duty free under these tariff items. I should like the parliamentary assistant to make that point clear. I am not disputing his figures, but I am definitely stating that his figures were at least misleading when he referred to the duty paid.
I should like to point out that importations of duty-free vegetable oils, including coconut oil and peanut oil used in margarine, increased rapidly during the first quarter of 1951. It increased to the point where-and the parliamentary assistant, through the extra staff he has over there, may check me; I do not want them to find themselves at leisure two-thirds of the year-an average of 1,531,000 pounds of margarine per month were imported in that period, as compared with an average of only 875,000 per month during 1950.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Public demand.

This was, on the average, an increase to the extent of more than 75 per cent. Mr. Speaker, all things come to him who waits: the parliamentary assistant has said, "public demand". That was the very thing I was hoping he would say. Here we have misleading statements issued to the public, that they are going to receive a food- and in this instance I will call it a food- as a substitute for butter, only to find it going to a very high price. "Public demand"-yes, by misleading statements, by bringing in oils duty-free, oils that can be turned in at one end of a machine and come out at the other, as I saw it done at the Canada Packers plant at Toronto. These oils are offered as a substitute for butter, for the production of which the farmer has to work 365 days a year, from twelve to sixteen hours a day. Yes, "public demand", when it is brought about by misleading statements that the consumer will get a cheap substitute. This oil, Mr. Speaker, was brought in and held in storage, duty
free. That was not told to the public. It was held over for this period until there was a short supply of butter and in order that five or six processors such as Canada Packers could profit, at the expense of the consumer. He did not get a cheaper substitute for butter. Canada Packers, duty free, got excess profits of ten cents a pound.
That does not appear in the record of May 17, at page 3122 of Hansard. I am willing to admit I may be prejudiced in the matter. I say I have every right to be prejudiced, on behalf of the Fraser valley milk producers association. Perhaps I am not qualified to give an impartial judgment in the matter, any more than the parliamentary assistant is qualified, with his prejudice in favour of Canada Packers or other manufacturers of margarine.
I am willing to admit I am prejudiced. I inferred from his statement that as a result of this freedom from duty the consumer would get the benefit in the price of the margarine which would compete with butter which was at an admittedly high price. He must have known, or his assistant must have known, that Canada Packers brought in this copra, this coconut meat, to manufacture into oils to be used in making margarine, that they held it from one to five months to sell at a rate ten cents greater than when they brought it in. If that is benefiting the consumer, then I would like to know it.
I am all for these preferential agreements and, in order to forestall what might be said, let me say that, with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), I am one of the two free traders left-and I know that will be thrown at me.
Here is another.
And here is another.

If I get a little more support, I will attend to this coconut oil, this poor substitute for butter. I want to tell you this-and I speak with authority from my own riding-that you can bring in margarine or margarine oil by the boatload, the trainload, by submarine or by aeroplane, duty free, if you will allow in duty free, under the same terms, everything that goes toward the manufacture of butter. When I say that I speak as a representative of all western ridings.
I do not care how much coconut oil you bring in duty free, provided everything we use in the production of butter receives the same treatment. I do not wish to delay the passage of the bill because, as I said earlier, I want to attend the sitting of the committee on veterans affairs. I can assure the house that although I disagree with mv

colleague, in most instances I have every confidence in his judgment. During the time when he served his country overseas we were assigned the same room, and I had the privilege of looking after his constituency. I trust no one will think there is anything personal in the present instance, because of the different views we hold in this connection. He is sincere in his belief, and I am sincere in mine-the only difference being that I know that, in the long run, for the benefit of Canada, he is wrong and I am right.
If the parliamentary assistant is going to speak I shall stay around and, if necessary, miss the meeting of the veterans affairs committee. Perhaps in doing so I shall keep the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) in his seat, because he and I might disagree in the veterans committee.
It sits tomorrow.

I am a day ahead of myself-but I am so anxious to help the veterans that it is possible I may be two days ahead. However, I shall certainly stay around to hear what the parliamentary assistant has to say.
Let me repeat that I have no objection to coconut oil or any other oil being brought into my riding in any quantity or in any form, provided those of us who produce butter and other dairy products in that riding are permitted to bring in under the same terms anything we require in the production of our dairy products.
I admit that if I represented a one hundred per cent consumer riding, particularly if I were speaking about the end of 1953, I might take a different attitude. But I would urge the consuming public to check the statements I have made today and previously concerning these imported oils. I repeat that the public was not given the benefit of these cheap oils in connection with the manufacture of this imitation of butter. But who got the benefit? Canada Packers and one or two associates got it, through holding those cheap, crude oils until such time as there was a scarcity of butter, arising as a result of the operation of the old law of supply and demand. When that shortage brought the price of butter to an admittedly excessive rate, the margarine was released.
The oil was produced and brought in, and the margarine was produced and held in storage at those ridiculously unfair competitive rates, and sold out at a 10 per cent increase. I have no intention of saying more.
I do not believe that the parliamentary assistant, in doing his duty as he saw it in his special capacity, intended to leave the impression that the consuming public of Canada was getting the benefit of these

Customs Tariff
imported oils. In Vancouver raw coconut meats were brought in and processed into coconut oil to manufacture this so-called imitation of butter, presumably for the benefit of the consuming public but actually to make excess profits for a few packing companies.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Order, if the parliamentary assistant speaks for the minister now he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I did not move the bill, but it is quite true that when the bill goes into the committee stage I shall be speaking for the minister. I should like to speak as the member for Coast-Capilano as well as the parliamentary assistant, and answer some of the charges my friend has made.

speechtext: I have not.

I believe we should abide by our usual practice and allow the parliamentary assistant to speak in reply on closing the debate.

That Is one of the
penalties of fame, Mr. Speaker.

There is one aspect of this matter that I should like to raise briefly. On a previous occasion we were told that the tariff reductions proposed in this bill have no reference whatever to the tariff concessions made at Torquay; the two are entirely independent. We were told the government was proceeding with these reductions without any regard for the agreements at Torquay or the course of the negotiations there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would the hon. member indicate when that statement was made, because I do not recall such a statement?

When we were debating the resolution, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) intimated, and my friend will find it in Hansard, that the tariff reductions proposed in the present bill have no relation whatever to the Torquay tariff concessions.

At that time it was also intimated, Mr. Speaker, that much of the benefit of these reductions will flow to producers in the United States. My point is this; why were the tariff reductions proposed in the present bill not used in bargaining at Torquay with a view to deriving further concessions, if possible, from the United States? If these were isolated in point of time, that is to say the tariff reductions proposed in the present bill and those proposed in the Torquay agreement which presumably are going into effect by order in council, then there might be some reason for saying that there was no purpose in using them as bargaining factors.
These reductions, however, come forward at the very time when the Torquay negotiations, having been carried through, issue in an agreement which was reported in the house subsequent to the introduction of and the debate upon the resolution which preceded the introduction of this bill. Now, putting those factors together, it seems to me only reasonable business sense that when the government was prepared to recommend the tariff reductions contained in Bill No. 295 it would have been desirable to try to get some balancing advantage for Canadian producers in the markets of the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the general position taken by the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). I believe we have made a serious mistake in allowing margarine to replace butter. What the producers of margarine did this spring clearly indicates what those gentlemen would do if there were ever a deficiency of butter, or if they ever got the herds of milk cows completely depleted. They would raise the price of margarine twice as high as butter ever went. These gentlemen who went into the manufacture of margarine did not do so for the benefit of the people, not by any means.
There is another serious aspect to this question, and that is that the dairy cow enriches the farm upon which she lives. She enriches everyone who has anything to do with her. The producer of margarine leaves the country poorer. There is not one single factor entering into the production of margarine that directly or indirectly contributes to the natural wealth of this nation. Let everyone bear that in mind.
I know the reason why a good many of our members were almost bludgeoned into supporting margarine. It was because the price of butter was so high people were groaning for relief. They wanted something cheaper than butter to eat.
The wise procedure for the government at that time would have been to subsidize the
Customs Tariff
price of butter in order to bring it down to a point where it could successfully compete with margarine. To try to talk any member of this government into paying subsidies however is just about as useful as trying to talk the mountain off its pedestal. Those gentlemen have not learned the elements of a sound economy. Until they do there is no use talking subsidies to them. Nevertheless, that would have been a sound policy, and instead of having 500,000 fewer cows in Ontario, we would have had 500,000 more. We would have been in a far better position to support ourselves than we are today.
I shall place myself on record as being in support of the position taken by the member for Fraser Valley in that we are not following a wise course in allowing margarine to displace butter in this country.

Mr. Speaker, the subject to which I wish to refer has no specific connection with margarine. I wish to refer the parliamentary assistant to a discussion which took place in the house on May 17 when we were in committee considering the customs tariff resolution. At that time I indicated a situation which had developed in at least one of our ports, namely, Sarnia. Certain purchasers of vehicles made in the United States had brought those vehicles into Ontario and paid the duty on them. When it became necessary to leave this province to proceed to Alberta by way of the United States, which is practically necessary under existing conditions, the owners of those vehicles were forced by the Canadian customs officers to post bonds to assure that the vehicles would not be sold in the United States.
Now, the assumption that they would be sold in the United States was fantastic, if not ridiculous. In the case of one vehicle, a hearse, a duty of $1,500 had been paid. It is utterly fantastic to believe that the purchaser, who was an Alberta dealer, would take that vehicle back into the United States and sell it at United States prices. On May 17 the matter was referred to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), because he said it was a matter of administration in the Department of National Revenue. The Minister of National Revenue asserted that there must have been some slip-up either in the information I received or on the part of the customs officers.
I have double-checked the information and I find that not only does this apply to the individual I mentioned, but on that very day -it was a Sunday morning-three other vehicles passed through and exactly the same thing applied to them. What I should like to do is to secure some information that can be

Customs Tariff
put on record in order to indicate to these Canadian dealers whether they may or may not drive these American made vehicles, upon which the duty has been paid, back through the United States. It would not have surprised me if the United States customs officials had insisted upon a bond, but they very quickly granted a permit. There was no difficulty whatsoever. The dealer in this particular case and the three individual purchasers were able to proceed through the United States without any difficulty at all. I think this matter should be cleared up because there must be a great many persons in the country who have posted bonds of $5 per vehicle. Actually it is not so much the matter of the $5 as it is the complete nuisance of having to do something which under the law conceivably is not necessary.

Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes I wish to speak in support of what the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has said this afternoon with particular reference to the practice followed in the months of February, March and April by margarine producers of raising their prices simply because, owing to a shortage of supply, the price of butter had increased. There is quite a large dairy industry in one part of my riding, and I find that the farmers' association has always taken a very reasonable attitude on this question. They have never previously urged me as their member to favour a customs duty on the importation of oils going into margarine until this occasion, when they now say: We think it is time that the public of Canada is placed in possession of all the facts, that it should no longer be represented that margarine is a cheap substitute for butter, one which will be available at a lower price and always at a lower price, and that therefore anyone who suggests that any difficulty be placed in the way of the manufacture of margarine is doing a disservice to the country. They now say: It can be seen quite clearly that these margarine manufacturers are quite prepared, as any other industrial manufacturer, to play the market for whatever it is worth regardless of the best interests and needs of the people of Canada.
I think the situation is now clear that our butter producers are entitled at this time to ask for a reasonable measure of protection and to request their members to ask the government as long as these-I do not know whether "unprincipled" is too strong a word;
I do not want to use over-strong words, but I shall call them callously indifferent practices -as long as these practices are carried on by the manufacturers of margarine, raising their prices when they had no increase in cost, then the government should be asked 
to afford some protection to the dairy industry. The replacement cost of margarine did not go up. The margarine manufacturers did not have to raise the price by reason of an increase in the cost of production.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Why did butter go up in the same period?

For two reasons which I would have thought the parliamentary assistant would have been aware of. One is the constant increase in the cost of producing butter, which is the thing that affects the farmers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not the manufacturer?

The second was the actual shortage of butter at that period. There was an increase in the cost of production, but it was not the farmer alone who was responsible for the butter price increase. It was the farmer to a very small degree who was responsible. I am not arguing for the big wholesale distributor who increased his price on storage stocks; I am talking about the dairy farmer whose industry has suffered as a result of this competition, competition which has been facilitated on the basis that it will be to the advantage of the people of Canada because they will get a cheap butter substitute. We find that when the margarine manufacturers get in the position they want to be in, and when there is no butter or very small supplies of butter available, then they increase their price although they have had no increase in cost. That is the situation to which I am objecting.
I object to this business for another reason.
I am not a tariff expert, and probably never will be, but it has occurred to me that the substantial changes in tariffs which have been made in late years have all been to the prejudice of the farmer. At the moment I do not want to enter into the controversy of high tariff versus low tariff policy. There is something to be said on both sides. Nevertheless it seems to me that, looking at the changes that have been made recently-the moves toward a low tariff policy-the majority of them have not been at the expense of the manufacturing industry but at the expense of the farmer. The small measure of protection which he has struggled for years to have built up-and I am thinking particularly of the dairy industry and the fruit and vegetable growers in our province- is now being whittled away.
As an example, I think particularly of the case of the apple industry where such measure of tariff protection as they had has been largely reduced over the last three or four years. Now we have the same thing

with respect to butter. I do not see why when we are moving, if that is what we are doing, in the direction of a low tariff policy, the first move should be made at the expense of the farmer, and that is what is happening at the present time.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Sinclair (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must inform the house that if the parliamentary assistant speaks now he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I will start by answering the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). He said that he understood that the tariff changes indicated in the bill were made without regard to Torquay. It is quite true that they were quite separate from the Torquay agreement but they were not made without regard to Torquay. Most of these items were used by our delegation at Torquay and they found they could get no concession in return for them. To give an example of the concessions we have made in this bill the extended concession on agricultural implements was raised at Torquay, and the United States representatives replied immediately: But it is the policy of your government to reduce and eliminate the tariff on agricultural implements. Why do you ask us to bargain on that?
Another concession is one which I remember very well. I raised the matter myself three years ago as a private member on behalf of the fishermen on the west coast. There was a tariff item that allowed the free entry of lines and nets if made from vegetable fibre. Most of the lines and nets were either linen or cotton. Along came nylon, and the tuna fishermen were the first to use nylon lines. Under our existing tariff the only way that nylon could be brought in was as lingerie. The fishermen and fishing supply houses very rightly objected to paying the tariff that applied to lingerie on lines which they were going to use for tuna fishing. I raised that matter because I represent a fishing riding.
It was one of the items also used at Torquay but used to no avail. We found we could get no concession out of them because it was generally known that the general policy of our government is to keep cutting down tariffs applicable to the fishing industry for the benefit of the industry. We thereupon removed the tariff here in this bill. It is not quite right to say that the amendments in the bill are made without regard to Torquay. They were items which were used without success at Torquay. Probably the major item so far as detail is concerned is the item in the present
Customs Tariff
measure having to do with all these parts of mining machinery j We had admitted mining machinery free. We had admitted integral parts free. We attempted to bargain on unfinished parts. Of course the United States representatives said: Obviously you are going to extend your policy to permit the entry of unfinished, parts, parts which you yourself can get manufactured in the same way that we are now doing.
With respect to what the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) said, first of all I must say that the figures I put on Hansard were correct. I was asked for the tariff on the oils generally used in margarine. These oils are usually imported in the refined state. As a matter of fact the total volume of imports of refined oils, edible oils, last year was three times the volume of raw oils. It is quite true that raw oils have lower rates. Raw edible oils from the British preferential countries come in free, and from most-favoured nations the duty is 10 per cent. The interesting fact, however, to show the extent of the division between raw and refined oils is that on all our edible oil imparts last year, raw edible oils which come in free from Great Britain and ait a rate of 10 per cent from the United States, and the refined oils which have the tariff that I enumerated at page 3122, the average tariff paid on all our refined oil imports last year was 13-3 per cent. The average tariff paid on all our edible oils was 16 per cent, so the tariff on the oils was very substantial.
I had rather expected that since the hon. member for Fraser Valley raised this question at some length during the resolution stage he would again raise it now, and I felt that perhaps the time had come to deal with this matter at perhaps greater length than would be normal. To begin with, both the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for Springfield have made the very flattering charge that I am responsible far margarine in Canada. Of course that is not so. Senator Euler very bravely introduced the question in the Senate for two years, and it was not until the third year that he picked me up as a recruit to introduce a bill in this house. As hon. members may recall, at that time my bill was talked out. That publicity may have helped to get results, but it was the Supreme Court of Canada which ruled that the federal ban on the manufacture and sale of margarine was ultra vires.
The second point raised by both the hon. member for Fraser Valley and his friend from Springfield at every opportunity is that margarine is unfit for human consumption.

On a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, if my colleague will refer to my speech today he will not find that statement. I did not say it was inedible. I said I was not arguing the merits or demerits of the product; the exact words are in Hansard. The rules of this house do not permit me to describe the qualifications or qualities of margarine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Of course the hon. member has substantiated my point. It may be quite true that in the present debate he has not made that statement in this house, but all hon. members will recall the statements by the hon. gentleman in recent months and years. Speaking as parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, who after all is responsible for the collection of taxes from both industry and individuals in this country, I believe as a measure of fairness to manufacturers who are making a perfectly proper and legal product and paying their ordinary taxes, and also to the consuming public who pay a 10 per cent sales tax on margarine and an average of 13 per cent on import duties on the oils used in its manufacture, I should refute this charge that margarine is not a good food, which is made here in the privilege of the House of Commons. I would like to turn back to the actual margarine debate, during which I put on record the opinion in support of margarine of the British medical association, the Canadian medical association and the Department of National Health and Welfare, which had issued a booklet even before the legalization of margarine in which they said:
So far as is known at present good margarine is a complete nutritional substitute for butter in an ordinary diet.
More than that, another authority came forward that day in the person of the Minister of Agriculture, whom I managed to involve in the debate and who agreed that he had never opposed margarine on the ground that it was not a good food. I would rather take the word of the British medical association, the Canadian medical association and the dietitians of Canada on this matter than the opinions of the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for Springfield. The manufacture of margarine in this country is a factory process, of course. It is an extremely hygienic process, as will be agreed by any M.P. who visited a packing firm on the Toronto visit, as I have not. That cannot be said for the manufacture of all butter in this country, as the hon. member knows very well. Very good creamery butter is made, but hon. members who remember the summer of two years ago will also know

that some very bad dairy butter is made in some parts of this country.
The same thing applies to margarine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
There has never been any similar objection to the standard of quality of margarine. However, I think the best evi-dance is supplied by the Canadian people themselves. The large consumption of margarine about which the hon. member protests is pretty good evidence to me of the quality of the product, and also of the need for the product. I believe that is indicative of Canadian acceptance.
Let us turn now and look at Fraser Valley, because most of us know that the interests of the hon. member for Fraser Valley are pretty well confined by the boundaries of that riding. I recall a debate some three or four years ago on the question of whether seiners or gill netters should be allowed to operate in a certain area of British Columbia waters, during which the hon. member made that very clear. He said that he had no seiners in his riding but that he had two gill netters.
The hon. member cannot put words in my mouth. I never said I had two gill netters. Unlike the parliamentary assistant, who is using his position-
Now, now.

If the hon. member for Halifax wants to make a speech in favour of the farmers, which I doubt, he is perfectly entitled to do so. The parliamentary assistant said I had said there were two gill netters in my riding. There are as many gill netters in my constituency, I think, as there are in his riding, but the pulp mills are not in my riding.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We are getting pretty far from the subject, I think. At any rate the inference was that whatever he had in his riding, he was for. He has made that abundantly clear since he has been in this house, as hon. members know. Well, I wanted to know whether the feeling in regard to margarine is shared by the people of Fraser Valley; and I go about these things in fairly objective fashion. I have a pretty good knowledge of my hon. friend's riding, since he is careful to invite me there during every campaign to help him get elected, despite the fact that I have championed margarine. I got in touch with the firm he continually denounces in this house and asked about their sales in the Fraser valley. Was this one dry spot, a dead end in which no margarine was consumed at all? I was somewhat surprised to get the reply that sales of

margarine in the Fraser valley were quite normal, that they exceeded sales in west Vancouver, my own riding, for example. I suggest that the hon. member need only leave his farm, the ivory tower in which he lives, and walk down to the little store in Clayburn and ask whether margarine is sold there. Or go to Abbotsford or Mission or to the dairy town of Chilliwack, and see whether or not they sell margarine. .Then he will know whether when he speaks in this way he speaks on behalf of all those people. The reason, of course, is that not all his constituents are dairy farmers. While he has many dairy farmers he also has a great many berry farmers and transportation workers, since he has the C.P.R., the C.N.R , the Great Northern and the British Columbia Electric. He also has a great number of sawmill workers, loggers-
Brick workers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, and a great number of old age pensioners and burnt-out veterans whom he defends so well in this house and who are very grateful for the opportunity to buy this lower priced substitute for butter.
At an increase of ten cents a pound.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I am being helped by the
hon. member, though I restrained myself from interrupting while he was talking. This increase was to match the increase in the price of butter. The hon. member apparently thought it was unfair for the law of supply and demand, which affected the price of butter, to also affect the price of margarine, though the manufacturer of margarine had the same increase in the cost of labour as did the farmer. In the case of the manufacturer this increase is supposed to be a heinous thing. Suppose we look at the dairy farmers themselves, and this is a very interesting thing about the Fraser valley. I have done a little research there. In Canada as a whole for every pound of butterfat sold in the fluid market two and a half pounds are sold for processing. In the Fraser valley that position is completely reversed. Two pounds are sold in the fluid market for every pound sold for processing; and the great bulk of the butterfat processed there does not go into butter but into condensed milk. I have the figures here for the first four months of this year. The fluid market took 2,700,000 pounds; for evaporated milk, 847,000 pounds; for butter, 390,000 pounds, or less than 10 per cent. Actually in British Columbia today we do not manufacture even 10 per cent of our butter needs. Most of the dairy farmers even in my hon. friend's 80709-234J
Customs Tariff
riding sell to the fluid market, or for processing into evaporated milk.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
And some of them buy
margarine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the next point I was coming to. I was particularly reminded of it when I was in Denmark a year ago on this military relief debt collection. At a dinner given by the minister to Denmark I sat next to a Danish cabinet minister. I had been driving around all afternoon seeing the lovely farms, and I was talking to the minister about butter and bacon, and we finally got around to margarine. He was surprised to find that we had had a ban on margarine in Canada. He said: Of course in Denmark even our dairy farmers eat margarine for two reasons. I thought I knew the first reason why any dairy farmer, especially a Scotch dairy farmer with a name like Sinclair or Cruickshank, would be eating margarine, and he agreed. The farmers took their butter to market, sold it at a high price and bought margarine at a lower price. But the second reason he gave was a most interesting one. He said: We Danes are a neat, clean, tidy, orderly people. If you saw their farms, you would certainly agree with that statement. I said, yes. He said: You know, some of our Danish dairy farmers always associate the taste of butter with the smell of the cow barn.

Will the hon. member
permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If it is pertinent.
Is it true that Denmark has the greatest percentage of defective eyesight among the children of any country in the world?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Knowing nothing more than
the hon. member's negative assertion, I would say that it is completely wrong. In any case, I want to close these remarks by reading some really good evidence of whether or not margarine is a palatable substitute for butter. We have had medical evidence that it is the nutritional equivalent. I have heard of this Toronto trip and of how members of parliament saw one of the larger packing plants in operation. They gave them a luncheon, and at that luncheon, I understand, margarine was served to certain members; and to confirm that, since the hon. member was attacking this company at every opportunity in the House of Commons, alleging that I was prejudiced in their favour, I wrote to them and on May 31 received this letter from the secretary of Canada Packers:
I have inquired into the Cruickshank affair and I find that he was served margarine at a luncheon

Customs Tariff
given in our dining room. I believe he was under the impression that he was eating butter, but such was not the case.

On a question of
privilege, Mr. Speaker, I want to say this, and I think I have the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) with me. There are certain privileged affairs, and I will bring as my witness the vice-president of the B. A. Oil Company, Mr. Godsoe, to confirm that I will go along with a gag. I will take anything at all, and I will pass it out too. I do not know whether the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff) and other Ontario members there did it as a gag. But this is appearing in Hansard and is going among the dairy farmers, and I do not think that even the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) wants to create a false impression. I was not served margarine; but as a gag a sign was brought in and placed at my seat at the table, owing to the fact that Canada Packers, in my opinion, showed poor taste, headed "serves farm members margarine." It was pointed out that it was set at my place after the dinner started. I say it is poor taste on the hon. member's part. I would not make this correction except for the fact that this is going out among the dairy farmers. It is said that this sign had been put at my seat at the table and that I did not know the difference. The members who sat around me know that I refrained from eating the margarine. I have a bet, any time that my junior colleague wants to take me up, that I know the difference between margarine and butter; but I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and through you the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, that when I am a guest at any function, I will go along with a gag, and I will not take advantage of any gag that is played. I think the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) will bear me out that I am correct in that statement, and I was a guest of the Toronto board of trade.

Speaking to the question of
privilege, along with some of the other members I had something to do with bringing the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) down to Toronto. It would appear to me that in writing this letter the company showed ill taste and bad manners. I think it was bad manners on the part of the company to discuss one of their guests privately. It is unforgivable to do it publicly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I may have made an error
of judgment myself in this. I should not like it to be thought that the company had. I made the inquiry but the secretary did not know I would use the information in the
[Mr. Sinclair.!
house. If it is distasteful to the hon. member, I withdraw my remark.
I hope however that this will put this debate on its proper footing. I must say the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) did try to argue whether or not admitting margarine as a reasonable substitute for butter had such an effect on the dairy industry as to seriously cripple it. That is the serious argument which should be advanced in this house on that matter. I would point out of course that margarine is the only major foodstuff which is subject to a sales tax of 10 per cent. Also, as I pointed out, the edible oils produced, both raw and refined, have an average tax of 13 per cent in point of duty. That is a substantial protection, I would think, for the dairy industry.
When he said that most of these changes in the tariff seem to be against the farmer,
I do not think the record quite bears out that statement. Over the years we have consistently removed the tariffs from agricultural implements at the request of farm members generally, and recently at his request and the request of the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness). They raised the question of the duty on portable sprinkling systems, for example, which we are now removing. As to the apple industry, and what they suffered last year, our exports to the United States were ten times our imports from the United States so the tariffs there cannot be said to be unduly severe in effect on the Canadian farmer. The general question of tariffs, of course, is a large one.
They took the market away from our potatoes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member mentions potatoes. The great value of our exports to the United States is in seed potatoes. We *cannot allow our large and profitable business in seed potatoes to be jeopardized by adjustments of other tariffs on potatoes generally. I think that situation itself has been up before the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on several occasions, and I think they are fairly content to have both arrangements working together-the concessions on seed potatoes to the United States, and the fact that Americans can send potatoes into this country. However, that is a fairly broad field and perhaps it could be dealt with better on the agriculture estimates rather than here.

May I ask the parliamentary assistant if he can give the ratio of edible oils imported to those produced in Canada? I refer to those which go into margarine. Is there an increase in domestic production?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
Carried.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will answer in committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think questions should be asked in committee.
I wanted to ask one question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The debate is now closed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

He referred to the increase in the price of margarine and rather brushed it off by saying that butter went up considerably and that margarine also went up because of the supply and demand. A few weeks ago butter went up about twenty cents a pound. It was followed right along by margarine to the extent of ten or twelve cents a pound. The question I want to ask the parliamentary assistant is this. Butter has gone back down again by about twenty cents a pound. Has he any information to give the committee as to why the full increase in margarine has still been maintained?

You know, when I was elected first in 1940 it was primarily to get the most I could for the dairy farmers and others within my riding; second, to work to the best of my ability on behalf of the province in which I reside and the surrounding ridings; and third, to work on behalf of the economy of Canada as a whole. It has been mentioned that margarine was sold in my riding, and I frankly admit it. It has been sold in my own little village of Clayburn; it has been sold in all parts of the riding, because unlike Coast-Capilano, where they depend to a great extent on the pulp mills

That is not the point, as I see it, and the point that has been overlooked by the parliamentary assistant in his exuberance to record on Hansard something about the hon. member for Fraser Valley who very seldom secures any publicity. He has overlooked and failed to answer the important point which was repeated by the hon. member for Kamloops, I believe, namely, that most of these oils that went into the manufacture of margarine had been imported duty free.
The parliamentary assistant made some reference to the fact that I had disputed his figures. I never disputed the accuracy of the figures as quoted by the parliamentary assistant. I think they are accurate. What I did say was that these oils came in duty free and were refined in Canada to go into the manufacture of margarine, and that immediately the price of butter went up the price of margarine went up by about 10 cents a pound, I believe, in spite of the fact that the oils used in the manufacture were to a large extent brought in duty free. I repeat, they were brought in at that time, held in storage, and then the margarine was manufactured. What the parliamentary assistant did not say was that when the price of butter went up- I believe it was in November-to the exceptionally high figure, two or three packing companies held the butter in storage and put the price up in the same way as they put up the price of margarine. The farmer did not benefit one cent from that increase. Make no mistake about that. I hope the people of Canada know that. That exceedingly high price of butter was of no benefit, but rather a detriment to the dairy farmer.
The dairy farmers in my own riding produce very little butter on the farms. We buy our butter. In other words we are consumers as well as producers. We produce milk for sale as butterfat, and we buy butter for our own consumption. We in the Fraser valley paid 81 cents a pound, or whatever the price was, for butter. And any farmer who was not in the fortunate position to be able to pay 80 cents or 81 cents a pound for butter bought margarine, and he paid this extra 10 cents a pound to this delightful colossus of Toronto, Canada Packers, over what they had produced margarine for. They themselves put the price of butter up because they and a few of their competitors were the only people who had
