I want to make it very clear that the consumers did not get the benefit, and the farmers who produced the milk for sale as butterfat did not get the benefit of the high price of butter. The dairy farmer as a producer bought butter in exactly the same way as the sawmill worker or the brick workers or anybody else, in most instances, at least so far as British Columbia is concerned.
The point I am particularly interested in is the importation of these oils in their raw state. It has been suggested, again I am sorry to say, by one member from my own province- I do not think he will make the statement in the province of British Columbia, even in a consumer district with the slightest hope of being re-elected-that this oil should be permitted in here to be refined. I well remember, Mr. Chairman-and it is exactly the same with butter as it is with fisheries-that two years ago I was lobbied in this house by a representative asking that we do not permit the fishermen in my riding, in Coast-Capilano, in Westminster and in two adjacent ridings, who produce fish, the primary producer, to send them eighteen miles to Bellingham where the fishermen would get from 5 cents to 14 cents a pound more, the argument being the same as that being used by these proponents of margarine, that if the fish were kept to the detriment of the primary producers, the fishermen in Canada, and manufactured into canned fish, or whatever goes with the byproducts within Canada, it would be to the ultimate good of the fishermen and the people of Canada. I was lobbied to that extent. When I am accused of primarily-perhaps wrongly-fighting for the interests of my riding, I have nothing to be ashamed of. speakeroldname: Mr. James Sinclair (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a motion to go into supply on May 23, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) raised the question of the statement made by me on the budget in 1949 with regard to the excise tax on watches. I promised at that time I would make a statement when we came to the second reading of the excise tax bill. Hon. members will recall that in the spring budget of 1949 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech said we were going to remove the 25 per cent retail tax on watches and jewelry and replace it by a 10 per cent excise tax on the manufacturers' level, and that the loss of revenue would be about $8 million.
The 25 per cent tax had been imposed during the war for two reasons, first as a revenue tax, and second to discourage the sale of these items during the war. That was followed by a resolution in the house which read in part as follows:
Resolved' that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide, effective on and' after March 23, 1949: . . .
2. That the retail purchase tax be repealed and replaced by an excise tax of 10 per cent, payable by the manufacturer or importer, on all articles now subject to the retail purchase tax.
Watches for personal use, other than watches for the blind and watches for railwaymen, had been subject to this 25 per cent tax. Therefore the question then came up of putting the tax back on the manufacturers' level. A problem immediately arose because of a practice by ten companies in Canada of importing not watches but watch works, watch cases and the actual final display cases separately. They said they were not importing watches, and I think most of us would agree. They then put the case and the works together, put it in the display case and sold it to the retailer, and , their allegation was that this was not the manufacture of a watch.
Well, to get away from all the legal technicalities, I think most hon. members would agree that no watch came into the country, if the case and the works and the

display case came separately. Hon. members would also agree that certainly a watch was delivered to the retailer by the people who brought in the parts; and the act of putting the watch together, if not manufacture undoubtedly was the production of a watch. With that in mind the Department of National Revenue, to carry out the terms of the budget resolution, sent a circular to the collectors of customs and excise, dated April 19, in the following terms:
The honourable the Minister of National Revenue has been pleased to establish the following regulations under authority of section 99, subsection 1, of the Excise Tax Act:
Regulations
On and after May 2,	1949, any person who
assembles clock or watch movements into cases therefor, and who adds any attachment, of metal, leather, plastic or any other material or combination thereof to a new watch, will be regarded as the manufacturer or producer of the clock or watch, as the case may be.
In other words the intent was in that order. Of course the fault in the order was that the resolution still had not been translated into an act and there was no authority to issue regulations, so these regulations could be more or less classed as a directive to the collectors of customs and to the watch manufacturing industries of Canada. They immediately protested, saying they were not manufacturers or producers of watches. They also said, of course, that they were not importing watches; and they urged that they should be freed from this 10 per cent excise tax. Ten of those manufacturers took this exception and held several meetings with the officers of the department. Those representations failed, as I think most of us would say they must fail. The parts came into the country; a watch was sold to the retailer. In the interval someone must have manufactured or produced a watch. The department said the person who put the case and works together had manufactured the watch, and it was at that stage that this 10 per cent excise tax was to be levied.
When these representations failed an appeal was made to the Supreme Court of Ontario on May 7. It asked two or three things. The key point, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Eglinton at page 3320 of Hansard, was the request for*a declaration that they were not manufacturers or importers within the terms of the resolution; that the excise tax was not applicable at the time of import, and that they were entitled to import without the manufacturer's or sales license.
The house prorogued without passing the budget resolutions, and the matter was then left in the position that the repeal of the
Excise Tax Act
retail purchase tax had been announced, and of course the jewelers of the country had stopped collecting that. The imposition of a 10 per cent excise tax had been announced on the goods formerly subject to the retail purchase tax, which of course included clocks and watches; but there was no law to enforce compliance by manufacturers or producers of those goods. The situation in this country has been mentioned many times in this house. The night the Minister of Finance makes his budget address he announces certain tax changes. Most of them come into effect at midnight that night. It is quite true that often weeks, and in this case from seven to eight months, elapse between the introduction of the budget by the minister, the introduction of the resolutions, the introduction of the bills founded upon them, the adoption of the bills by the House of Commons and Senate and royal assent; but it has been the custom in this country since confederation that when these tax changes are announced by the minister they are regarded as being in effect from the time the minister indicated they would be. If subsequently, though this has never happened, the house should not approve the tax changes contained in those resolutions, of course the manufacturers and others who had paid those taxes would be entitled to refunds. Actually, of course, the practice is that the house has always endorsed the principle of those resolutions as contained in the bills, and the tax collection has been proceeded with.
We came back, then, in the fall; the budget was re-introduced, and the resolutions were re-introduced. Because of this question whether we had the right to regard the assembly of the case and the works as the production of a watch, and to make it quite clear that we were going to regard that as the manufacture or production of a watch, the new resolution specifically mentioned that fact. The hon. member for Eglinton called my attention to it when I was putting the resolutions through, and I said we thought we had that right anyway, as was shown by the regulations which were sent out in the form of a circular, but that to make it quite clear we were spelling it out in the bill. But in order not to prejudice the ease then before the courts we agreed to have this specific wording apply only from November 10, when the matter came to the public notice with the first reading of the bill.
I want to recapitulate the position of the government up to that time. The minister brought in the budget and announced that the retail sales tax of 25 per cent was to be dropped and an excise tax of 10 per cent was

National Defence
to be put back at the level of manufacture on those items. We had sent out a directive to the customs collectors and the industry and had actually started to collect the tax from nine of the ten watch manufacturers. This was appealed to the courts, and the case was before the courts when we re-assembled in the fall. To make it quite clear that henceforth we intended to regard that as manufacture we spelled it out in the bill. speechtext:
I wish to announce a substantial addition to the existing program for the construction in Canada of ships for the Royal Canadian Navy.
Orders have heretofore been placed for the construction of twenty-seven vessels for the Canadian navy on which work is now proceeding. The estimated cost of these orders already placed is ninety-six million dollars.
The additional orders now being placed total approximately sixty million dollars, and provide for the construction of twelve more ships. Included in these orders now being placed are seven destroyer escorts in addition to seven already contracted for; one loop layer; two steel crane lighters and two modified Norton class tugs. Of these new vessels one additional escort vessel will be constructed by Marine Industries Limited, Sorel, P.Q., where one escort vessel has already been ordered. Canadian Vickers Limited, Montreal, Halifax Shipyards Limited, Halifax, and the Burrard Drydock Company Limited, North Vancouver, will each build one of the escort vessels now being authorized, bringing
[Mr Sinclair.]
to a total of three the number of ships of this type being built by each of these firms.
Three shipyards which have not previously received orders for escort vessels are each undertaking one of the remaining three. These are Yarrows Limited, Victoria, B.C.; Victoria Machinery Depot Company, Limited, Victoria, B.C.; Davie Shipbuilding and Repairing Company Limited, Lauzon, P.Q.
The loop layer will be built by George T. Davie and Sons Limited, Lauzon, P.Q.
One steel crane lighter will be built at the Pacific Drydock Company Limited, North Vancouver; the other at Saint John Drydock Company, Limited, East Saint John, N.B.
The Saint John Drydock Company will also build two Norton class tugs.
The placing of the orders above mentioned brings the construction program for the Royal Canadian Navy to date to a total of one hundred and fifty-six million dollars covering the construction of thirty-nine ships.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'olock I had been discussing the case which was referred to in Hansard as the Gruen watch case and which was raised by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on May 23 when he alleged bad faith on the part of the government with regard to the undertaking given by myself as parliamentary assistant in the budget debate in the fall of 1949. I had reached the point where the ten watch companies had met with the government and then decided to file suit. Before suit was filed, however, five of the companies withdrew. They had been paying the taxes. One of the companies which withdrew was the Gruen watch company, and I believe they feel it is rather unfair that the case that went to the supreme court and to the court of appeal should be referred to as the Gruen watch case, because they accepted the ruling and had paid their taxes.
Chief Justice McRuer gave a lengthy judgment, of which I shall quote only two little parts that to me as a layman seem to be the pertinent ones:
The effect of the provision that sections 5 and 6 should come into effect as of the tenth of November, 1949-
That was the undertaking I gave in *the house so as not to prejudice the case which was then before the courts.
-for the purpose of this case is to leave it open to the court to decide whether the other retroactive aspects of the suit in fact apply to the plaintiff.

When he talks about "other retroactive aspects", he is talking only as far as the court of law is concerned; because when the minister on budget night in the spring had announced the changes, as far as the country was concerned the changes were in effect that night. It has been the custom since confederation to accept those changes as of that night, although the actual legal royal assent did not come until the bills had gone through both houses of parliament some time later.
Then Chief Justice McRuer goes on to say this:
I cannot find that the simple operation of putting a watch movement into a watch case is manufacturing a watch in the ordinary popular and natural sense of the word, but I feel clear that the plaintiff produced watches adapted to household or personal use.
I now come to the key part of the judgment:
X therefore find that for the purposes of the Excise Tax Act the watch movements as imported were not watches.
And we agree with that.
That being so, the inescapable conclusion is that the plaintiffs by importing movements and placing those in watch cases so that they might be convenient and1 useful for personal use as watches are producers of watches adapted to household or personal use and therefore are now liable to pay excise tax and sales tax pursuant to the retroactive provision of the amendment of 10th December, 1949, on deliveries made to purchasers on and after the 23rd May.
And then the last part of his judgment which appeals to me:
Having found that the plaintiffs were producers of watches adapted to household or personal use since 22nd March, 1949, under the state of the law as it now is they have been liable to pay the excise tax according to the terms of the statute since that time. No useful purpose could be served by making a declaration that they were not liable to pay the tax until the statute of 1949 with its retroactive effect had received the royal assent.
Note the words "that its retroactive effect".

But again the retroactive effect is not the effect of the amendment I moved in November, 1949. The retroactive effect he is talking about is the effect resulting from the fact that the act did not receive the royal assent until December, although the intent of the budget and of the resolution had been stated here by the minister on March 23, that spring; and the custom of Canada since confederation has been to put these taxes in effect immediately until such time as the act is passed. That is the retroactive effect to which Mr. Justice McRuer refers. He makes it clear that he is separating the amendment which was proposed by
Excise Tax Act
me from the other inevitable retroactive effects from our way of implementing the budget resolutions.

The court of appeal-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
In March, 1949, the Minister of Finance stood up and mentioned many tax reductions. One of them was the removal of the 25 per cent retail tax on watches back to 10 per cent excise tax at the manufacturers' or producers' level. That reduction was a saving of $8 million to the taxpayers of Canada and it was certainly welcomed by the watchmakers of this country because the 25 per cent retail tax was a nuisance tax which interfered with sales. As is the practice under our way of bringing in budgets since confederation, those tax changes went into effect that night. It is quite true that as far as the law is concerned, they did not become law until royal assent had been given to the excise tax bill which in this case did not happen until December 10 of that year.
Nine of the companies paid their taxes. A case went to the supreme court on the claim of the Bulova watch company, first of all, that they should not have that excise tax levied on the works, case and the display case which they imported separately. But that was not a watch. We all agree that that was not a watch, we who are not lawyers. However, when the case, watch and works were put together and sold to the retailer, it certainly was a watch; and the Department of National Revenue, in their directive to the trade in April, said that that process was going to be regarded as the production of a watch and that 10 per cent excise tax was to be levied there.

The companies protested. Naturally they would like to avoid taxes-not evade taxes but avoid taxes. After discussion with the department six of them went to the supreme court and the chief justice ruled in effect that we did not need that fall amendment spelling out precisely that the assembly of the case and the watch was the production of a watch, but that the spring resolution had covered this point. He ruled that the intent of the change in March placed that tax at that production level. The case was appealed to the court of appeal by just one of the ten companies. I may say that nine of the ten companies have paid the tax without question. To the ordinary person not versed in law it would be inconceivable that there should be any place where a tax could not be placed on that watch; if we did not tax the separate parts coming in and did not tax them as they come together, then that watch could be placed in the hands of retailers without that excise tax which is levied on other producers and manufacturers.	[DOT]
There was no bad faith on the part of the government; there was no tearing into shreds and tatters the good faith of parliament. The provision which I made at the direction of my minister was that since there was this case before the courts we would spell out this expanded resolution to make it clear that we did so regard the assembly of the works and the case as the production. If then the courts, on the basis of the spring resolutions, should say that this was not the production of a watch, then from November 10 on we would collect because of the amended resolution. As it turned out, the chief justice ruled that that was the production of a watch, and so the excise tax was properly levied at that level.

Perhaps worst of all, it is just not possible to believe that you can have any sort of effort at government economy when all these hundreds of millions are floating about. The sad thing naturally that one always has in mind is that these increases of surplus never come from less spending; they always come from taking more of our money. Of course these sales and excise taxes put up prices. Then the increased prices put up taxes, and so on and so on, and we have this terrible spiral.
I just want to make the point that everything we predicted on the 16th of April has happened. Prices have increased just as we said would happen. The surplus is here just as we predicted would happen. Wage demands are here just as we predicted would happen. I suggest that the happenings of the last six weeks have greatly strengthened what we said at that time. For that reason, and in order that we may express our continuing disapproval of the sales tax, I am going to move:
That the word "now" be left out and the words "this day six months" be added to the end of the question.

I hope the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will agree that is very different from what he thought it was going to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is in order. Let us have the question right now.

Mr. Speaker, we had a long discussion of the sales tax in the debate earlier, but nevertheless I believe the protest that has been made tonight is worth making again because in my opinion the sales tax is probably the most oppressive tax that we have, and to raise it from 8 to 10 per cent at this stage is bound to increase the cost of living further. The cost of living index has reached the unprecedented figure of 182 points on the 1935-39 basis. That in itself is something that should cause us to stop and think when we are imposing a tax which is bound to increase the price of many commodities. It will not increase all commodities, and indeed not some of the basic commodities, but still it will increase the cost of many of the commodities that enter into the cost of living for a good many families in this country.
I think it is true to say that, no matter who suggests it, the sales tax is a tax which is unfair. It taxes those with families who have responsibilities that are escaped by those who have no families. It seems to me that the sales tax is a thoroughly bad tax. Tonight the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has raised the question of the surplus that the government was able to show in April. Since that large surplus was shown at that time, it seems to me to indicate that the country can do without the 25 per cent increase in the sales tax suggested in the budget. Consequently, without prolonging the debate, because I think most of us said all that it was necessary to say at an earlier stage, I am merely going to say that we shall support the amendment moved because we believe that the recent receipts of the government indicate that we can dispense with this tax, and whether it is a good or bad tax we should dispense with it on that account. Secondly, because this is a tax which is liable to increase the cost of living in so many respects of those who are least able to afford it, I think the house is justified in asking that the imposition of this tax be deferred.

Mr. Speaker, I said at one time that I was so much opposed to this tax that I felt I should talk against it until next Christmas if necessary to have it held up or to oppose it so successfully in that way that the government might decide not to pass it. The government has very obligingly suggested today
Excise Tax Act
giving me a couple of months to get my breath so that I can go on talking about it this fall and probably right up until Christmas. I will continue to do so on every occasion that I have the opportunity. I am opposed to the imposition of the increase in the sales tax, and I have not found anything yet in reason, logic or argument to make me change my mind. When it comes to voting on the bill I shall know what to do about that section particularly, but as to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), since it appears to cover the whole bill it might make it very difficult for some hon. members to support it because there are things in the bill that are good, and I should like to see them passed. Therefore I shall have to think much more carefully than I have thus far as to whether I can support the amendment.
I rose tonight to speak briefly about another provision in the bill, and I can make a much more informed appeal than I was able to do on May 1 on behalf of many thousands of suffering Canadians. On May 1, as hon. members may recall, I raised a question, as recorded at page 2599 of Hansard, as to whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would consider adding the substance known as vitamin E to the list of tax exempt substances now taken care of in section 12 of the bill. At that time the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) said:
Wheat germ is the cheapest one there is.
I said:
Yes, it may be the cheapest, but this particular one is subject to sales tax, and the tax increases the price to a considerable extent. It puts it outside the reach of many patients.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Not at all. You can get all the
vitamin E you want in wheat kernels.
We continued with an exchange of views, and it appears that neither of us knew very much about it at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Speak for yourself.

Well, I shall give evidence to show that the doctor did not know what he was talking about. Mind you, I want to say to begin with that I am not blaming the Minister of National Revenue for not being able to keep up with the latest discoveries in medicine because-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Much less yourself.

-he is so completely occupied with finding ways and means of exacting taxes and finding the best means of collecting them that he cannot possibly keep up with these things, and I would not expect him to. However, the question I must ask first is: What is the material about which I was asking on May 1? I

Excise Tax Act
was referring at that time to high potency vitamin E concentrate which goes under the scientific name of di-alpha tocopherol. Wheat germ oil contains minute fractions only of vitamin E. If a patient has to take 300 international units of vitamin E daily, which would be about the equivalent of 300 milligrams, and that by the way is an average dose-
If the hon. member will permit, he did not mean 300 kilograms.

No, I said milligrams. Certainly I would not say kilograms. I say if a patient is to take a prescribed dose of about 300 international units or the equivalent of about 300 milligrams of vitamin E, and has to resort to wheat germ oil to fulfil this dosage, he will have to consume in one day more than a quart of wheat germ oil. I am sure the Minister of National Revenue knows the ill effects that would follow; neither his stomach nor mine could stand it. I would go further and say that this quantity of wheat germ oil simply could not be tolerated by any person. This patient would require at least 150 capsules of ordinary vitamin E such as you buy in the drug store today to make up this dosage; and the cost of those 150 capsules would probably be as much as $7 a day, which would be simply prohibitive.
High potency vitamin E is a concentrate that is obtained through a process of molecular distillation of the oils of cottonseed, peanuts and green vegetables. It appears to be manufactured by only one firm; that is Distillation Products Incorporated, a subsidiary of the Eastman Kodak Company of Rochester, New York. It is therefore imported into Canada in large drums and then encapsulated into 75 milligram capsules. The population of Canada is not sufficient to warrant the huge expenditure required for the manufacture of alpha tocopherol.
The second important question we have to ask ourselves is, what is the product used for? Well, Dr. Evan V. Shute and his brother, Wilfrid E. Shute, discovered after years of research and clinical work that vitamin E in heroic doses, that is in huge doses, was very valuable in the treatment of heart and circulatory diseases. These doctors then founded the Shute institute for clinical and laboratory medicine in London, Ontario, and have been carrying on successfully since. These doctors prescribed a dosage of from 300 to 400 international units daily for victims of cardiovascular ailments, which of course would include thrombosis, Buerger's disease, thrombophlebitis, indolent ulcers, angina and hypertension. These are the diseases which, if the present trend continues, 
will take off every other person in Canada who is now over 40 years of age. That is the record to date; that seems to be the trend.
Since the Shute brothers discovered the value of alpha tocopherol in the treatment of cardiovascular ailments, many doctors of this country and the United States and other countries have taken up the research. In many countries they have issued their bibliographies, and their findings have been almost identical with those of the Shute brothers.
The next question is how widely is alpha tocopherol distributed. This substance, as I said, is high potency vitamin E. How widespread is its use today? Well, one pharmaceutical house I asked told me they did not know exactly but their records alone indicated that many thousands of cardiac and vascular victims are resorting to high potency vitamin E with success. They know from their records that several thousand doctors in Canada are prescribing alpha tocopherol, after the Shute therapy, to their patients. To their personal knowledge over 1,500 doctors and most of the major hospitals are prescribing vitamin E; and remember, this pharmaceutical house is only one of thirty Canadian pharmaceutical firms distributing vitamin E products in Canada. I am convinced that more than one-third of Canada's nine thousand doctors prescribe it today for therapeutic and for what may be called prophylactic treatments. What is more, of the more than six thousand patients on the files of the Shute institute at London, more than 160 are medical doctors and members of the immediate families of doctors. Just here I should like to put on record a telegram I received from Dr. Nelson George, because it indicates what doctors themselves think of this thing:
As a physician practising in London for thirt) years would like to record my experience with vitamin E. Have been a diabetic for twenty years. As a result five years had a hemiplegia with residual weakness left leg and arm. One year ago for diabetic gangrene had right leg amputated above knee. Last fall when amputation of left leg imminent for diabetic gangrene I began vitamin E treatment under Dr. Shute's care. Left leg healed rapidly and has regained function so that I can now stand on it unassisted. I am no longer a diabetic, no longer a hypertensive. Want to stress that as physician had best care available in London yet continued to be a diabetic and hypertensive and eventually developed gangrene with their care; lost the first leg above the knee. On vitamin E gangrenous area healed and filled in; had partial restoration of function, absent for five years. Am no longer a diabetic and no longer a hypertensive. The necessary dosage of alpha tocopherol (vitamin E) was 450 international units, about 150 times that available in one capsule of wheat germ oil with latter cost $7.25 daily, with imported concentrated brand retail cost 54 cents a day. No human stomach can tolerate that much vitamin E in form of wheat

kernels, wheat germ or wheat germ oil capsules, 150 capsules daily. My wife has been my nurse since my amputation. She is willing to appear before you or Dr. McCann or the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am willing to be interviewed by any member of dominion house.
That is from a doctor who himself has had the treatment for some time, and who cites the results. Just here I might comment briefly that heart ailments are the greatest killer of all. One-half of the adult population of this country will meet untimely death as the result of one form or other of vascular trouble. Doctors especially find themselves susceptible to these diseases because of the very high tension under which they have to work.
The next question is whether there is scientific backing for the claims made for this product. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is not claimed that high potency vitamin E is a perfect answer to the problem of heart disease. It is not, and that is frankly admitted. But it is therapeutic; that is, it has curative value. That has been amply demonstrated in extensive research using nine different species of animals, as well as in the treatment of thousands of cases among human beings.
There is another side to this question. If alpha tocopherol is used prophylactically, that is for preventive purposes, it should achieve considerably more than it has been able to achieve in the treatment of advanced cases of heart disease. It appears that the real future value of the vitamin E product will be in the preventive field. The preventive use of alpha tocopherol might well begin in childhood, and the Canadian public should be educated to this kind of medical insurance, which to my mind it certainly is. At the same time Canadian millers might be induced to make available to the public a cereal flour rich in germinal vitamins.
There is a mass of pertinent evidence to support the assertion that the appalling mortality among men resulting from heart diseases has arisen from a deficiency of alpha tocopherol in the diet. In other words Canadians have been slowly starving themselves into sudden death from thrombosis or a more lingering and painful demise from angina or hypertension. The greatest single factor contributing to this slow starvation and early death is a deficiency of vitamin E. Many thousands of Canadians suffer from chronic deficiency of the alpha tocopherol type of vitamins in their diet. The substance is found widespread in certain natural foods but its principal sources are in the cereal grains. Modern milling, in the effort to achieve a stable, exportable flour that will not turn rancid, and which will have a fine, white
Excise Tax Act
appearance, has taken out all of the germ of the cereal grains. Consequently there is a vitamin E deficiency in the diet of the people.
Chronic shortage of vitamin E of the alpha tocopherol type damages the heart muscles and the walls of the arteries of the circulatory system. If our Canadian people, from their childhood, would use whole wheat bread made from freshly-milled whole grain flour and plenty of fresh vegetable oils, it is practically certain that untimely deaths from heart disease would be many times reduced from the number that are experienced amongst our population today.
It is not surprising that so many of our people are having to resort to a therapeutic treatment based on the use of the vitamin in which their diet for many years has been tragically deficient. I might say here Mr. Speaker, that there are analogies in medical science to the use of heavy doses of vitamin E in the treatment of heart disease. In particular I would remind the house that, for instance, in cases where insulin shock results, physicians prescribe high and heavy doses of insulin to cure it. There are other analogies that I could cite.
I do not want to take too much time, Mr. Speaker, but what about the price to the people who use this product? I was able to obtain this product that I hold in my hand for the purpose of showing it to the house. I have no particular reason for naming this particular one other than that I could get it quite easily. What about the price to the people using what is known as Webber Vita E capsules, as an example? And by the way, hon. members can see the size of the capsule I hold in my hand. The capsules are a fairly good size; and they contain 75 milligrams or 75 international units. Using that one as an example, the retail price per 100 of these 75 international unit size capsules is $9. The retail price per 1,000 of the same size is $80. The return to the manufacturer is $4.50 per 100 or $40 per $1,000. The sales tax is paid by the manufacturer and is absorbed into the general price structure. The sales tax in this instance is based on the lowest discount price. It is not based on some of these other prices I quoted, but on the lowest discount price and1 therefore amounts to 10 per cent of $4 when one is buying a bottle of 1,000. But if the sales tax were removed from this product, there would be a saving of $4 per 1,000 to the wholesaler, which would mean a saving of $8 to the consumer, on 1,000.
Here is a right good example of the way in which a sales tax at the manufacturer's level pyramids prices. To be able to secure "gelucaps", as these things are called, the

Excise Tax Act
government causes the heart or vascular patient to have to pay $8 in increased prices. That is a terrible thing.
In addition to the sales tax, this product, and all others of the same class, are subject to customs duties of 15 per cent, because there seems to be only one source, namely, Distillation Products Inc. of Rochester, N.Y., It is imported into Canada as a concentrated oil in large drums and then is made into capsules for distribution to patients. Duty involves another 60 cents at wholesale level, or $1.20 at retail level per 1,000.
I have been puzzled a great many times as to why the government should require customs duty to be paid on a product of this kind; I refer to vitamin E concentrates. It has never been manufactured in Canada. That being so, the product is not competitive from the tariff point of view. I was always under the impression that tariffs were designed mainly to protect our basic manufacturers. In this particular instance, no Canadian manufacturer is protected and for that reason, it seems to me, the consumer, the heart patient, carries an additional burden for no good reason at all. The reason for removing the tariff as well as the sales tax from vitamin E concentrates would appear to be quite obvious to even the most casual thinker. All in all, the patient-consumer can save $10 per 1,000 by the removal of the sales tax and customs duties on this particular product.
Let us now take a look for just one moment, in conclusion, at the daily cost of this material to the patient. The prescribed dose may run from 300 international units to 450 international units a day, or 4 to 6 of these gelucaps of the size of the one I have in my hand. On that basis the present cost to the patient would be 36 cents to 54 cents a day when buying them by the hundred, or 32 cents to 48 cents a day when buying them by the thousand. It is clear that the present cost to any patient is a very heavy burden for him to bear. It must be remembered that cardio-vascular patients must continue to use the product every day of their lives, just as is the case with insulin and diabetics. It is a pitiful thing, to me at least, to learn of patient after patient who has been unable to earn money for months or years, has a family to support, and yet feels that somehow or other he must get together enough money to buy his vitamin E at the rate of 32 cents to 54 cents a day. Persons in that .situation either go without the necessaries to do this or find they must discontinue treatment and lapse into illness as a consequence.
Today I am making an appeal to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on behalf of

the thousands of Canadians who are suffering from cardio-vascular ailments. I ask the minister to add vitamin E-that is high potency vitamin E; the type known as alpha tocopherol-to the list of drugs to be made sales tax free. I appeal to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and ask him to remove the customs duty on this item which must be imported from the United States. I want to thank the two ministers and their colleagues-and I do so sincerely- for what they have done for arthritics and other sufferers by removing the sales tax from such things as ACTH and cortisone.
I think that is a step in the right direction. But at the same time I urge them to learn about vitamin E and the beneficial results it brings to heart patients. Here is a chance, it seems to me, to help thousands of worthy Canadians at very small cost to the government by way of lost revenues.
Just in conclusion let me say this. There is in Canada today an association known as the Vitamin E Association. It so happens that one of the members of this house is one of the high officials in that association. They call it the Vitamin E Society of Canada. Its headquarters is in Toronto. If that gentleman who is one of the high officials-in fact, he is the president-cares to speak, he could tell you tonight that his wife, who was for many months on her back, helpless, with heart disease, and given only 3 months to live in the opinion of heart specialists, was taken to the Shute institute and after a few months of treatment with alpha tocopherol was able to get up and be around, and is now holidaying, or was a short time ago, in California and was getting along fine. There are others in the house who have had experience with the product, and who could speak of the benefits from its use. Certainly it would seem to me to be a case worthy of most real and earnest consideration, and I ask that of the ministers tonight.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the house will support the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). Any doubt that hon. members opposite may have had a month ago in regard to the imposition of the 25 per cent increase in the sales tax must surely have been removed in the light of the statements issued since then from the treasury.
In his budget address the Minister of Finance proposed such taxes should be levied as, according to his figures, would produce at the end of the fiscal year a surplus of $30 million. The figures that were released for the month of April have shown an astounding result. After paying all expenditures for that

month, the first month of the fiscal year, the minister has reported a surplus of $121,520,000, just four times the surplus in one month that he budgeted for for the entire twelve-month period. It is not sufficient, Mr. Speaker, for the Minister of Finance to say:	Oh, well, this picture may
change before the end of the year. I submit that we have here already a very fair test of the kind of budgeting that has entered into the calculations of the Minister of Finance in the course of which he has asked this house to authorize the imposition of greatly increased taxes, particularly of the most objectionable of all varieties, at a time like this, which will increase the cost of living of those least able to bear it, taxes also which are subject to the vice of taking far more out of the pockets of the consumers, the ultimate consumers, than are yielded to the treasury in tax revenue.
Let us compare these figures with those of the first month a year ago and, sir, in approaching those figures let us have this in mind: most of the increases in taxes which are contemplated in the budget resolutions, and part of which are provided for in the bill now under debate, had not come into effect in the month of April, so that what we are dealing with in these figures for the month of April are taxes levied chiefly at the rates prevailing in the fiscal year which closed on March 31 last. There is very little of the increases in taxes, even in those indirect taxes, that find their way into the figures to which I am now about to refer, and none of the increases in the corporation taxes and in the personal income taxes of course become effective until July 1.
I think the dating of some of these taxes is worthy of note. People, of course, are not going to be too conscious of these indirect taxes because they are going to be covered up. That is one reason the government likes taxes like the sales tax and the excise tax, which they have increased so substantially. They are covered up, and the people who pay them are not conscious of the fact that they are paying them. The people are conscious of paying taxes like the income tax, and so the government has provided that these increases in the direct taxes, of which people will be very conscious, will not take effect until July 1. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it is a mere coincidence that four by-elections take place in this country on June 25, just six days before these increases in the direct taxes come into effect.
Sir, the figures for the month of April, to which I am about to refer, are to be found in the issue of the Canada Gazette of May 26, 1951, at pages 1502 and 1503. There we shall
Excise Tax Act
see that on the revenue side the minister's receipts in April, 1951, as compared with April, 1950, are increased on every item except two. I will just give the nearest figure in millions. First, the customs import duties show an increase. They are doubled from $14 million to $28 million. The excise duties are increased from $14 million to $17 million. The excise taxes are increased from $13 million to $24 million. The income taxes on individuals show large increases. Deductions at the source are increased from $12 million to $26 million. Other collections, that is, of income tax against individuals, are increased from $37 million to $44 million. Corporation taxes are increased from $38 million to $60 million. Succession duties show a slight decrease from $5 million in April, 1950, to $3,500,000 in April, 1951. Miscellaneous tax revenue has increased from $10,000 to $21,000. Postal revenue has increased from $6,500,000 to $7 million. Return on investments shows a slight decrease from $3,600,000 to $3,500,000. Miscellaneous non-tax revenue has increased from $320,000 to $601,000. The total receipts of ordinary revenue are increased from $147 million to $217 million. There is a decrease in special receipts, and the total revenue figures show April, 1950, $166 million; April, 1951, $218 million.
What is going to happen, Mr. Speaker, to these swollen figures when the full effect of the proposed increase in taxes of the Minister of Finance reflects itself in the figures for succeeding months? These figures are going to engage in a runaway race from last year's figures, and next year we shall inevitably again face the picture with which we have grown altogether too familiar: the Minister of Finance coming in with his budget and claiming great credit to himself for showing a surplus far in advance of that pictured to the house when the house approved his tax proposals the previous year. That is not sound budgeting. If the Minister of Finance will include in his budget proper provision for debt reduction, I am sure the house will be glad to consider any such proposals on their merits, but this indirect way of doing outlandish budgeting, which builds up surpluses far in advance of those offered to the house by the Minister of Finance in inviting the house to approve his budget proposals, is completely unsound. I submit, Mr. Speaker, the time has come when the house must say, this must stop. When we see figures like these for the month of April indicating how far the Minister of Finance has erred in the figures that he put before the house in his budget speech six weeks ago, then I think the house will start right now on this bill and say, we are not going to impose these heavy tax increases on people

Excise Tax Act
who are having really a desperate time to meet the soaring costs of living. We are not going to do it when the Minister of Finance cannot prove need.
Sir, the figures that were announced for the month of April also reflect increases in expenditure for the month of April over those of a year ago, $88 million in April, 1950; $97 million in expenditures in April, 1951. So, let it not be said that the weight of increased government expenditure has not been reflected in the April figures. The $121,500,000 surplus of revenue over expenditure in April last as compared with April, 1950, takes into account increased expenditures, and reflects in only a very minor degree the increase in taxes, the full weight of which will be felt by the people of Canada on and after July 1.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if there was abundant reason before for rejecting this increase in taxes, particularly this sales tax, this most inflationary of all the budgetary weapons being wielded by the Minister of Finance on the people of Canada today, there is infinitely stronger reason for rejecting this increase in taxes today.
It is well to bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the statistics just released by the dominion bureau of statistics show another increase in the cost of living for the month of April. It is true it is a much more modest increase than those we have been accustomed to in recent months, but the fact of the matter is that even though the cost of living index has shown a slight decrease in the figures of the cost of food, the total cost of living for the month of April has shown another fractional increase, and we are now faced with a situation where the cost of living is higher today than it was when the budget resolutions were adopted. In the face of all these facts surely the house will not be party to imposing these cruel increases in taxation when there is no need of them.
Having appealed to the house to support the amendment of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), which is intended to defeat these proposed increases in the sales tax, and which is intended to offer to the people of Canada such protection as parliament can offer them against an increase in this inflationary sales tax, I turn now to the subject discussed by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance.
Let me say in the first place that I do not think it was altogether fair of the minister to leave these matters to his parliamentary assistant because there are errors I think that the-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
He handled it very well.
TMr. Fleming.]

There are errors the parliamentary assistant has made unintentionally in connection with the interpretation of the judgment to which he referred.
I do say, however, in regard to the case put forward by the parliamentary assistant tonight on behalf of the government that it is a most disappointing answer, and shows that apparently the government is entirely unrepentant in its denial of justice. It is entirely unrepentant in its breach of faith with the house. And mere sophistry of the kind we listened to this afternoon and evening, however plausible it may sound, is no answer to the indisputable fact that the government, in permitting the parliamentary assistant to say what he said to the house on November 30, 1949, and taking the stand it has taken today, and which it has consistently taken throughout the litigation in the courts, is breaking faith with the House of Commons.
The parliamentary assistant did not say very much in his speech today about the undertaking he gave the house on November 30, 1949. He did not read the text of it to the house. He rather put a gloss on his remarks containing that clear and unequivocal undertaking which was accepted by the house at face value. And so we have a sort of paraphrase on the part of the parliamentary assistant tonight of what he said on that occasion in clear and unambiguous words.
The parliamentary assistant has sought to argue the government's case against the watch companies. The only thing wrong with the way he argued it tonight is that it is entirely contrary to the way the courts decided it. The courts had before them the legislation and the facts to which the parliamentary assistant has made reference. They had all those before them; and having heard them all, and having duly heard the extended arguments of very eminent counsel on both sides as to the proper interpretation of the relevant portions of the Excise Tax Act, especially the 1949 amendments, reached a decision quite at variance with that offered to the house tonight by the parliamentary assistant.
The net result of the litigation is that the courts have held that these plaintiffs were entitled to everything they asked for in the action which they brought in May of 1949 for a declaratory judgment. They were entitled to everything. And now, in the net result, the courts have felt obliged to deny to these litigants the fruits of their action, the rights to which they were entitled, simply because this house enacted an amendment on November 30, 1949, which it not only

did not understand it was enacting, but which is just the very opposite of what it was told was the effect of the amendment being introduced by the parliamentary assistant at that time on behalf of the government.
The parliamentary assistant has said this afternoon-and he is referring here to the statement he gave to the house as to the effect of the amendment which he was undertaking, in the discussion of section 5 of the 1949 amendment, to introduce at a later stage of the bill-
But we said we would not prejudice the case then before the courts.
The government has said through its spokesman today, referring to what was said in the house on November 30, 1949:
But we said we would not prejudice the case then before the courts.
Sir, that is precisely what the government did. That is precisely what the government did in misleading the House of Commons as to the effect of the amendments which the house was being called upon at that time to enact, and which the government then put into operation in this legislation with the avowed purpose-there could be no other- of repudiating its own undertaking.
They have said here, as they said in the house, that those amendments would not be made retroactive to have a bearing upon the litigation then before the courts. All that is asked, all that is required in the name of simple justice and decency and good faith is that the government should make good what it said, namely that it should not by the amendment of November, 1949, or the use it instructed its counsel in this litigation to make of the amendment, prejudice the case then before the courts.
But that is precisely what the courts have found that the government has done. The parliamentary assistant has undertaken to interpret the judgment of Chief Justice McRuer. Let me stop to put him right upon that by referring to two brief passages in the judgment where the learned chief justice said:
I place my judgment on the claim set out In paragraph (a) of the prayer on the footing that the retroactive provisions of the act of 1949 apply to the plaintiffs . . .
The whole point which the parliamentary assistant has missed is that as the resolution stood when introduced on the eve of an election in March, 1949, and left suspended in mid air during the election campaign and until November, it could have no bearing to create a tax liability on the part of persons engaged in the kind of business that these plaintiffs were engaged in. Then when parliament is invited to enact an amendment to the act on
Excise Tax Act
November 30, 1949, this question is raised: Will the amendments which are being put before the house now have any retroactive bearing on the case then before the courts? Let me read what was said in the house at that time. I said this, as reported at page 2503 of Hansard for November 30, 1949:
Sections 5 and 7 are related for the purposes of the matter I should like to raise, which has to do with the imposition of an excise tax on the assembly of watches, clocks and certain kinds of jewelry. If I am correctly informed, this has become the subject of litigation as well as having been agitated by correspondence with and representations to the government. I understand that this litigation is pending and I am concerned as to whether this legislation will not cut right across the issues involved in the pending litigation which directly concerns the government.
The answer of the parliamentary assistant, as I have said, was clear and unequivocal in these words:
The hon. member has put his finger on an amendment which I propose to move a little later. It is quite true that a case involving sections 5 and 7 is now before the courts, but I would direct his attention to the fact that section 14 provides for the coming into force of sections 5 and 7. When that section is reached I propose to have a minister move an amendment which would change the present date of March 23, 1949, to November 10, the date when first reading was given to this bill. There would then be no retroactive effect which would have a bearing on the cases before the courts.
And, sir, the courts have held that that is precisely the effect of the amendment, that it does apply to the cases in court, that it has a retroactive effect, and that it defeats the claims that the plaintiffs in the litigation would have been entitled to recover but for the imposition or enactment of this retroactive legislation in breach of the undertaking given to the House of Commons by the government.
The parliamentary assistant has apparently overlooked the fact that, as to those matters in which Chief Justice McRuer held the plaintiffs not completely entitled to the remedy they sought in their action, the Court of Appeal supplied what was lacking, because the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal of the same litigants as against the crown, and held that the plaintiffs were completely entitled to all aspects of the declaratory judgment which they sought. The only thing that defeated these litigants was this retroactive legislation enacted by parliament in the very teeth of the representations made to the house at that time in the clearest possible language. The Court of Appeal went so far as to award the costs of the action against the crown. Let me read these excerpts from the judgment of the Court of Appeal of Ontario to put right the statement made to

Excise Tax Act
the house this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant, who trespassed too deeply into interpretation of the decision of the court. This is the decision of the Court of Appeal, and it was a very strong five-judge court. As you well know, Mr. Speaker, a panel of five judges is assigned in the Court of Appeal of Ontario only to cases of leading importance. This is a unanimous decision of the five learned justices of appeal, and these are excerpts taken from the judgment of the court as read by Mr. Justice Aylesworth. He says:
I think that the case is clearly one in which the appellant is entitled to the formal declaration of the court as to its rights. So far as now relevant the declarations sought for, in essence, would assert that the appellant is entitled to secure entry through customs of certain component parts for watches without payment of excise tax upon such entry and without the issue of a manufacturer's and1 an excise licence for that purpose.
Then he makes reference to the pleadings, and in speaking of the rights of the plaintiffs he says:
Those rights, in my opinion, should have been and ought now to be stated by way of formal declaration in the judgment itself.
Then he proceeds to indicate in detail the various provisions in the declaratory judgment to which those litigants are entitled. What has happened, Mr. Speaker, is that a strong court in the Court of Appeal of Ontario, with a full panel of five judges, has said that these plaintiffs are entitled to everything that they sought in their action, and they would have had everything, had it not been that those rights were handicapped by retroactive legislation passed by this parliament. Now, that fact is crystal clear, and it will not admit of any attempt at being denied by the kind of sophistry offered to the house this afternoon and this evening by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance.
Sir, the only reason that this result has occurred, that this blemish has been cast upon the honour and good faith of the crown, is that the amendment introduced in the house on November 30, 1949, by the parliamentary assistant was not as he represented it to the house. I do not say that he intentionally misrepresented it to the house. I do not suggest that. But the fact of the matter is that the house was completely misled. The effect of the amendment, as the courts have found, so far as its retroactive application to litigation then pending in the courts was concerned, was directly opposite to what was represented to the house by the parliamentary assistant. Nothing could be plainer than this very contradiction between what the courts

have found to be the effect of this amendment, and the effect of it as represented to the house by the parliamentary assistant.
When this matter was under discussion a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), whose department is responsible for applying these amendments to defeat the effect of them as stated in good faith to the house by a spokesman for the government, on that occasion said, "Well, why did you not check on that amendment to see that it went as far as represented?" Mr. Speaker, when a plain statement of fact is made to the house by a spokesman for the government, in words as unequivocal as those appearing at page 2503 of Hansard of November 30, 1949:
There would then be no retroactive effect which would have a bearing on the cases before the courts,
the house should be entitled to rely on it. This discussion was in committee, and that assurance was followed two pages later by a statement on section 14 of the bill by the parliamentary assistant. I raised my point on section 5, and it applied as well to section 7. The parliamentary assistant suggested we wait until we come to section 14, at which time he had an amendment he was going to introduce which would meet all the objections. He then said:
There would then be no retroactive effect which would' have a bearing on the cases before the courts.
The committee then reached section 14, and the parliamentary assistant rose in his place and said:
This is the section on which the minister will move the amendment about which I spoke in answering the hon. member for Eglinton. The amendment is as follows:
"That subclause (2) of clause 14 of bill 175 be amended by striking out the words 'second day of May' and substituting therefor the words 'tenth day of November'."
That is the date when this change first became public knowledge by reason of the first reading of the bill.
Then Mr. Howe says, "I so move." The amendment was agreed to, and the section as amended was agreed to. Sir, no member of the opposition saw that amendment. You know what happens in committee on matters of plain amendments where the effect of the amendment as stated by a government spokesman meets the wishes of the house. An amendment is introduced in due course, and time does not permit copies to be circulated to all members so that they may study the terms of the amendment. It was an amendment that sounded plain enough to carry out the intent as declared by the parliamentary assistant, and with that unequivocal statement by the parliamentary assistant that this legislation would not have any retroactive effect, surely the house was

entitled to rely upon it. But what was overlooked, Mr. Speaker, was a very tiny amendment that should have been made in the schedule of the bill. This tiny amendment was overlooked. I am sure it was not overlooked deliberately by the parliamentary assistant, but the government has since completely ignored the unequivocal terms he used in referring to the amendment. Notwithstanding that, this government has completely broken faith with the house; it has tarnished the good faith of the crown by the course it has followed by trying to wrench these 1949 amendments to defeat the claims of persons who were told by the language used in the debate in the house that there would be no retroactive application to their cases.
I was not the only one, sir, who made representations to the government against making these 1949 amendments applicable so that they could have any bearing on the litigation before the courts. When I spoke on this subject recently I said an hon. member who was then a private member of the house on the other side, and who is now a member of the cabinet, also made representations, because he sent a note over to me on the occasion when the parliamentary assistant made his statement in the house intimating to me that he got word a few minutes before that this amendment was being introduced, and that it was in fact a triumph for justice.
There were other private members who were consulted about this, who made representations to the government to the same effect, and who understood, as every member of the house understood, that the parliamentary assistant was stating the fact when he made the representations to the house to which I have referred. I should like the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) to say something in this debate about what he thinks of the way in which the government has wrenched and distorted these amendments enacted in November, 1949, in the very teeth of the statement made on behalf of the government as to their effect. I should like to hear what the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Rooney) has to say about it, and there are other members of the house who interested themselves in trying to see justice done so that legislation would not be enacted so as to have a retroactive bearing.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has said with a measure of glee that to begin with there were ten of these companies who were plaintiffs in the action, that four of them withdrew before the case came to trial before Chief Justice McRuer, and that only one of them carried the case
Excise Tax Act
to the Court of Appeal. He puts that forward as a reason, if you will, why parliament should acquiesce in this breach of faith. Because one out of ten had the courage to carry his case to the Ontario Court of Appeal the parliamentary assistant says that the course of the four who did not go as far as trial is the best indication of what was fair or unfair in this situation.
I think it is to the highest credit of that one litigant who, not daunted by the dangers of standing up to the government in litigation, had the courage to take his case to the courts until he got as much justice as the courts were in a position to give him. I think it is a matter worthy of the highest commendation on the part of this house that any litigant, that any subject of the king, be he person or be he corporation, is not daunted by the totalitarian juggernaut of government, but is prepared to take his case to His Majesty's courts looking for justice, and justice would have been done in this case if the courts had been free to apply the law as parliament understood it and as the government represented it to be. Nothing could be clearer.
Sir, the story does not end there because, you see, the government disapproves of the action of this one litigant in carrying his case to the Court of Appeal. They disapprove, perhaps to a lesser degree, of the action of the other five who went as far as trial but did not join in the appeal. You see when governments-this government at any rate-disapprove of the action of a subject they can if they are vindictive enough make life pretty miserable for him because every individual in this country has to have relations with the Department of National Revenue. I find that a known subsidiary of the litigant that was successful in the Court of Appeal is already having its problems trying to obtain an appointment with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) to discuss its legitimate tax problems on which they require an interpretation, but the Minister of National Revenue says that he sees nothing to be gained by discussing this question with them. The door of the Minister of National Revenue is apparently now closed to this litigant and its subsidiary corporation.
Sir, the story does not end there. This trail of vindictiveness is pursued. It happens that the very distinguished and eminent counsel who appeared for this plaintiff in this case- and I may say he is a very well known Liberal -was at the same time and has for many years been counsel to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and, if you please, recently he has been notified by the Canadian

Excise Tax Act
Broadcasting Corporation that they will not have occasion to require his services in the future. Is it mere coincidence that it is through the Minister of National Revenue that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is supposed to be responsible to parliament? It is this same minister who has been responsible for the position taken by the crown in this litigation in breach of faith with this house.
Sir, there is a tarnished record. There was a time when the honour of the crown was regarded as something unimpeachable and without blemish, but in the hands of this government the honour of the crown has been tarnished and has been blemished. Nothing will remove that tarnish on the honour of the crown except to do justice to these litigants. Even then this government will have fallen far short of repairing the breach of faith with this house. What ought to happen is that the government, speaking through the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), should offer an apology to this house for a palpable breach of faith with the house. Those who are responsible from the minister down should be brought to book for being parties to a breach of faith practised upon the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it must be a source of regret to many hon. members of this house, and I hope not entirely on this side of the house, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) should not have seen fit to deal with the statement that has been made.
A reflection on the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I hope he will still come in before the debate ends on this stage of the bill because, as one of the members just opposite has said, it is a reflection on the government. It is a reflection on the government that a lawyer of the standing of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) should place before the house clear and unchallengeable statements as to undertakings that were given, and that the minister responsible should not see fit to answer those very serious charges, dispose of them, and not leave it to his assistant who, whatever his qualifications may be, is not competent to interpret the legal aspects of this question.
The statement has been made, and made with clear reference to the Hansard record, that assurance was given that the legislation then before the house would not have the effect of depriving litigants, whose cases were then under consideration, of the rights they possessed. Nevertheless in the manner

that has been described the result of amendments introduced at that time was to deprive these litigants of their rights. I wish to reemphasize what has been said by the hon. member for Eglinton. Far from being any answer to the clearly described impropriety of the government's action in this case, the argument put forward by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance this afternoon only aggravates the situation. He tells us that of ten companies who were seeking to be relieved of the effect of that legislation, only one carried the case to appeal. Far from being a source of satisfaction to the government, that should be recognized as a reflection upon the whole attitude that is developing and the fear that is being aroused in the minds of corporations that if they do assert their rights they will suffer in some other way at the hands of this government. Let no one be under any illusions that all that took place in connection with those cases was what was discussed openly in the courts of this land. One company did have the courage to carry the case forward, and the judgment in that case made it perfectly clear that no matter what the original intention actually was on the part of those who presented the amendment, the effect was directly contrary to the undertaking that was given.
The case has been clearly stated by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) with the legal ability he is known to possess; but apart from the legal considerations there is the fact that unless this is to be more satisfactorily dealt with than it has been, unless it is to be dealt with by the minister who is competent to do so from the legal point of view as well as from the standpoint of governmental responsibility, which is also something the assistant cannot do, then we are left in the position that members of this house are unable to accept any assurance given by the assistant to the Minister of Finance. That carries us right to the present position. Either the minister backs up the statements of his assistant or he does not. If he does not we are no longer in a position to rely upon the assurances given in that way. So we have the two aspects, one the wrong that was done at the time this amendment produced a result entirely contrary to what was stated, and the second the fact that unless this is dealt with in some way we shall be unable to rely on further assurances that may be given.
We are now dealing with legislation that will have far-reaching consequences, legislation which calls for assurances of various kinds, particularly when we are in committee. The effect of this statement is all too

much like the statement already referred to: "If we wanted to get away with it, who would stop us?" The government feel they can get away with it, and challenge anyone to stop them. That attitude apparently is not confined to one minister or one department, if this matter is allowed to stand as it is now.
To come to the question of the bill now before the house, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) has introduced an amendment asking that this bill be not proceeded with. One hon. member who indicated his objection to certain of the contents of this measure also indicated that he had some reluctance in supporting this motion because there were things in the bill of which he approved as well as those of which he disapproved, and evidently for that reason he felt that it was not appropriate to support a motion which obviously would have the result of deferring consideration of the bill in its present form. On the second reading of a bill it is not possible to rewrite the legislation, nor is it possible to change the detail. I submit to all hon. members, however, that if there is in the bill something manifestly unsatisfactory, it is perfectly proper that a vote should be cast against the bill containing those unsatisfactory features. I would point out that in addition to the increase in sales tax there are reasons which suggest the advisability of deferring consideration of this measure. As has been pointed out already by the hon. member for Greenwood, the surplus already disclosed by the Department of Finance indicates that the increase in the sales tax as well as other provisions are not necessary to raise the money required to meet the budget that has been placed before the house. Therefore the government would be in a position to concur in a motion of this kind and re-introduce a bill deleting those provisions. By doing so it would impose only those taxes which it is now clear will be adequate for the purposes of this budget, and that is all the government should seek to raise.
I would point out that in addition to the sales tax other matters have been mentioned which are included in this bill. No satisfactory explanation has yet been given of the prejudicial attitude taken toward electrical appliances, as indicated by the fact that cooking stoves which do not use electricity do not pay the extra tax, while cooking stoves using electricity have to pay this special tax of 25 per cent. In this country we have every reason to encourage the use of electricity, particularly in the rural areas, because of its economy and simplicity. Far from discouraging the use of electricity, the taxation policy of this government should recognize
Excise Tax Act
the extent to which electricity is bringing better living conditions in many parts of Canada.
Going beyond that, however, it is difficult to see how the distinction was drawn between those things regarded as luxuries and those things not so regarded. In the first schedule of the act, for instance, we find that electrical appliances of various kinds carry this special 25 per cent tax. There may be those who will agree that curling irons or tongs may be in the nature of a luxury. There may be those who will agree that food or drink mixers are in the category of luxuries. But surely irons and ironers, kettles, toasters, washing machines and things of that kind are no longer luxuries in this modern age. To go further into the provisions of schedule I, we find that such things as stoves, hotplates, grills and other appliances when adapted wholly or in part for cooking and when designed for using other than solid fuels, are included. They must be designed for cooking. Is the government trying to stop people cooking in their own homes? There seems no other reason for the special provision that they must be designed for cooking if they are to carry this tax. If they are not so designed the tax does not apply. This whole thing seems to be approaching the requirements of our people in these days from the wrong direction.
I want to refer further to some of the provisions in schedule III. We find that where a stove has two kinds of cooking facilities the part using electricity is taxed while the part using solid or other fuel is not. In other words if we import coal or oil, as we still do in substantial quantities in this part of the country, stoves using those fuels are not taxed. But if we use our own electricity for cooking, those stoves are taxed. There has never been a more unreasonable, impractical application of taxes in this house than this provision with respect to cooking equipment.
Of course, if the answer is that it is intended to cut down on the use of steel, then perhaps it might be interesting if the minister or someone competent to speak on behalf of the department would tell us why it is that, as an example, there is no tax of this kind on filing cabinets which use more steel than any of these cabinet arrangements of this kind which will be taxed in this way but are used in the home. While we have wood that we grow, and while as yet there appears to be no critical shortage of wood, I suggest that we should be discouraging the use of steel in filing cabinets and boxes of that kind more than its use in

Excise Tax Act
refrigerators, washing machines and things chat people use in their homes in these days.
These provisions are covered in this bill. They are bad, and for that reason a blanket opposition to this bill is sound, although there may be some features in the bill which are perfectly good. But then we come back to this sales tax. The minister himself made it perfectly clear that even though a tax can be justified up to some point, there comes a point beyond which it is no longer sound to keep extending that tax. When it was suggested by some members of this house that possibly the tax on alcoholic beverages might have been increased, the minister explained that there is a point beyond which taxation of that kind cannot go and still be sound. In saying that he recognized the fact that a tax may be justified, in the opinion of the government, up to a certain point, but that at some point it ceases to be a sound tax.
I am not prepared to concede the soundness of the sales tax at any point, no matter how much it may have become embedded in our system. We all recognize that some of these things that are carried on for years are difficult to dislodge. But if the government has passed the point where it is sound to increase taxes on alcoholic beverages, certainly it has also come to a point where that principle should apply with equal force to the things that people are buying for their daily needs in these days of increasing inflationary pressure.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the only way that the members of this house can register their objection to this further increase by 25 per cent in the sales tax at this time is to vote on an amendment which indicates that the bill should not be proceeded with at this time.
