That is the amendment before the house, and it is one which I would hope we would see supported by some of the hon. members in this house who do not sit on this side of it. By the announcement that has been made as to the surplus for the first month, the government have demonstrated that they do not need this inflationary tax-this tax which bears most heavily on the people least able to afford it, this tax which mainly soaks the poor-when they already have for one month a surplus that would nearly equal the total amount they are going to raise in this way. On further consideration I hope that other members of this house, besides those who have already indicated their support of this amendment, will speak on behalf of their people who should not be called upon to pay this tax.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the question is put, Mr. Speaker, I should like just about two minutes. I think the house should realize that during the period of a little over four months during which we have been here for this session the cost of living index has risen by 9-5 points. I ask the house to compare that rise in four months with the fact that during four years, from 1941 to 1945, the rise was only 7-8 points. In four months this year we have had a greater rise than we had during the whole four years under price control.
That fact supports the argument that we in this group have been making, namely, that price controls and subsidies are necessary. We still call for their introduction. The government has the power to take action, and we contend that it should be taken. But at the moment what we have before us is this bill which, amongst other things, imposes this drastic increase in the sales tax. It seems to us that the least that parliament should do at this time, in order to try to check this rising cost of living, is to reject this proposal for increasing the sales tax. It is because the amendment now before the house is intended to express the opposition of members of the house to that increase in the sales tax that I for one feel that the amendment should be supported.

I supported the budget when it was passed here; but after listening to some of the arguments advanced tonight, I think there is a good deal of merit in what the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) said. I have been here since 1945. I know that is a short period, but in that period it seems to me that we have collected from the Canadian taxpayers about one and a half billion dollars more than we as a parliament have sanctioned.
I admit that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) should probably be congratulated on having achieved these surpluses. I will admit that he is probably being honest when he tells us that he did not expect them and that he gave us an honest guess. But to be quite frank, it is almost impossible for me to realize that the minister and the high-class talent that he has around him in preparing these budgets could be so far wrong, particularly last year with the $343 million surplus, I think it was, that we had. It seems to me that it is more than was justified under the circumstances.
Actually he comes out finally with a surplus of $203 million. But he could give away $65 million to the wheat farmers. That was a good garbage can in which to hide some of his surpluses. He found he could spare another

$75 million to put into the civil service superannuation fund. I wish he had told me he was getting rid of some of these surpluses, because I had several suggestions as to where he could put some of them; there were things in which I am interested, including the pilotage fund as to which I heard the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) say that he felt that the government could not afford any assistance at this time.
I think at times we are probably a little bit unfair to the minister. He is a modest chap. He always tries to make being Minister of Finance seem the simplest thing in the world. I often think that it would be better if he were like our former ministers of finance and had a long beard or something. Maybe he would look more profound. But I think that we have for too long taken the easy assurances of the minister. He says: We are going to have a $20 million or a $30 million surplus this year. It seems to me that may be true if he is able to hold the cost of living and the present purchasing power of the diollar, something which I do not think he or the government is at all certain of.
I am a great believer in balanced budgets. But it seems to me that this one and a half billion which we have collected-which the minister has not anticipated-since the war, could probably have been used by Canadian investors in this time in acquiring interests in our Labrador iron, for instance, or probably in our Alberta oil fields.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: For debt reduction.

Debt reduction in itself is a fine thing. But I would point this out to the parliamentary assistant. He is a young man. He may have read at some time what was said by Henry Ford, a very wise old man. Henry Ford said that he would advise every young man to go into debt when he was young and then to get himself out of it in due course when he was able to do so. I feel that in Canada today we have a young country. I should like to see the capital that is put into Canada put in by Canadians. Certainly we are not going to do it if we take one and a half billion dollars more than we need out of the Canadian public. Actually, I think the cabinet should be very much concerned. They know very well that the $2 billion surplus that they have collected from the Canadian people has been collected since the war as the result of inflation. We can say that in some measure they are responsible for it. I realize it is a world-wide condition, and I would expect that prices would go up to some degree; but when the government sits back and very complacently says, we have $2 billion surplus, and are very proud of it, I say that the only reason that they have got
Excise Tax Act
the surplus is not through extra good management of Canadian affairs. I can tell you that. I do not think anyone in the government would be complacent enough to say that. The reason you have it is that there has been a drastic reduction in the purchasing value of the Canadian dollar, and as a consequence there has been a greater dollar volume of business going through.
Have we not prosperity?

We certainly have prosperity. I am very glad to say that we have that factor in our economy, but a little criticism of this government will not hurt it. They are safe in their position, and there should be a little sound criticism of the government.
What I would like to point out to the government is that since they have this money I wish they would use it with as much of their infinite skill as they display in collecting taxes, and try to get some of the money that they have collected fortuitously from the Canadian people by reason of inflation back to the people who are suffering the most in this country from the effects of inflation.
When the late prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, introduced his first proposal in regard to pensions in this house, which was sanctioned by the cabinet-I imagine it must have been-he suggested that we were just going to raise the veterans pensions by 11 per cent. Everybody on the government side thumped his desk and said that that was fine. It did not seem quite as much as it was expected. After a while quite a lot of criticism developed in this country and then they put the ante up to 17 per cent. Finally we came down here and we put these pensions up to 25 per cent where they should have been in the first place. We find now that the same thing is taking place in the veterans affairs committee. There is to be a means test. I would think the government would be wise to take this $2 billion which they have accumulated since the war and see if they can get some portion of it back into the hands of the people who have suffered the most from inflation.

Was the hon. member in the
house at three o'clock?

I have no illusions as to
where the money is coming from for old age pensions. I certainly hope the government has enough common sense now to realize that the $350 million for old age pensions has to be collected out of the people who are going to receive them. Do I understand from the hon. member from Spadina (Mr. Croll) that we are not going to finance this currently

Excise Tax Act
as we go, or are going to dip into our past surplus? I do not think so. I just feel the government should be very careful now. We have this surplus of $2 billion now, and it looks as if we are going to have a very substantial surplus again this year, judging by the way the figures are going. Quite frankly, I am not sure that the minister himself needs this extra 2 per cent sales tax to get the surplus that he expects to have. For the salutary effect it might have on the government I am going to support the amendment of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell).

The
principle of this bill is that certain forms of excise tax ought to be levied on Canadian commodities in order to raise certain sums of money from Canadian consumers for the defraying of divers governmental expenses. The stated or implied reasons for such procedure are:	First, that the withdrawal of
active purchasing power from circulation to the extent of the sums involved will constitute anti-inflationary measures. Second, that the acquisition by the government of the sums of money involved is unsound unless such money is obtained either through taxation or borrowing. I personally challenge the validity of each of these two reasons.
I personally contend that the cause of the high prices presently prevailing in Canada is not scarcity of goods in relation to the money in active working circulation, but that the cause of our so-called inflation has been deliberate profiteering forcing up costs of production. As I have pointed out, the first step in this spiral of inflation was the deliberate advance of $5 a ton in the price of steel, permitted by this government in 1946, and it had nothing on earth to do with the money in circulation, or the scarcity of steel or the inability of Canadians to produce more steel; and the increase in wages by reason of the strike in the steel works in 1946 again forced up the prices, and had nothing on earth to do with the surplus of purchasing power in relation to the goods.
That same principle followed all the way through will explain the rise in prices right up to the present time. And why it is that it takes so long for so man}' people in Canada to see that is beyond my comprehension. To imagine that we can force back the price of steel for instance by any degree of taxation in this country is simply fantastic.
I personally maintain that the sums of money proposed to be raised by the imposts contemplated through these taxes in this bill can be safely taken from the Bank of Canada, and spent into circulation by the government without inflationary effects

through monetary influences. I do not say that doing that will keep people from stealing from each other if you permit them to increase their prices beyond what they have a right to increase them by; but I will say that if suitable control measures are adopted there will be no inflation by taking that money from the Bank of Canada.
My reason for this assurance is that the supply position in Canada at present is such that the said sums would be absorbed by surplus goods existing in Canadian inventories in May, 1951, and coming into existence through Canadian productive facilities now in operation. I therefore personally oppose the principle of this bill.
I maintain personally that Canadian supplies are as adequate as I have indicated. Some of the reasons why I believe this I propose to give. I may be wrong. It is difficult for us to be sure about the supply position in the country. I can go only by the evidence we are able to obtain. Of course, if there is not enough supply in Canada to support the money I propose, then something would have to be done in the way of controls and even rationing in order to prevent a rise of prices because of too great demand for the supply.
I have already referred to the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on April 9 as reported at page 1762 of Hansard. May I read it once more:
I am sure that we can get along quite comfortably as consumers and still engage in a substantial defence effort. A few things may in the course of time become unavailable or relatively scarce, but standards of living will remain high. Unless all-out war comes, Canadians can continue to live well.
These words have only one possible meaning, coming from a man as cautious about his wording as is the Minister of Trade and Commerce. They must mean that the supplies are adequate in Canada. If they are, I maintain the money can be created by the Bank of Canada, can be borrowed from the Bank of Canada by the dominion government and spent, without any such iniquitous taxes as are proposed in the present bill.
Let us look at some of the details in respect to supply. How are we off for food in Canada? I am getting my information from an authentic letter of May 16, 1951. Production and supply of most foods is well ahead of a year ago. What about flour? Well, it is reported to me that our flour supply was up about one-third' in January. What about other cereal products? They are in good supply. What about our fluid milk? Temporarily down, because of foolish governmental mismanagement, but I am told there is a long-run increase. What about butter? No real scarcity. We have made a mistake. In connection with

margarine we have made a serious blunder in respect of our dairy industry, but we can easily retrace our steps and undo the blunder. What about beef? There has been a governmental mistake again in connection with beef. But it certainly is possible in Canada to produce enough beef, and if we cannot now produce enough beef we can ration it until such time as we do, in the future, have enough beef.
What about pork? I understand our pork supply was ten per cent higher this year in January than it was last year. There was almost a one-third increase in stocks in Canada. What -about fish? I understand that landings were 12 per cent higher and that storage was 15 per cent higher than in 1950. What about eggs? I am told that the shortage of eggs -at the present time is largely in reference to the export of eggs, but that we have plenty of eggs for the home market.
What about sugar? Production and supply are ahead of what they were. Stocks in January were over 30 per cent higher than they were before. What about potatoes? Everyone knows what happened to potatoes. The supply is far in excess of what we are able to use. What about fruits and vegetables, canned and fresh? We have -a larger supply than we had last year and it is ample.
What about prepared foods and beverages? The same applies to them. Our supplies are ample for our requirements. What about clothing? In connection with cotton yarn, I am told that we had 20 per cent more bales of cotton opened in 1950 than in 1949. That does not indicate a shortage of supply. We may be selling a good deal of it abroad, or using it in other ways. But, so far as the supply is concerned, we are in a sound position. We had a ten per cent higher opening of bales in January 1951 than in the preceding January. We have increased our yarn and our cloth supply.
What about our woollen supply? I understand that woollen cloth shipments were up about one-third in December of 1950 over the previous year, and our inventories were up a [DOT] quarter. That does not indicate a shortage of supply.
What about hosiery? Shipments had increased by one-quarter, and stocks also were higher. What about knit goods? The same is true as in the case of hosiery. What about boots and shoes of all kinds? They were higher in the last quarter of 1950 than in the year earlier.
Then, what about housing? Here is a general comment on housing-and let it be
80709-23G
Excise Tax Act
understood that I am not defending the housing situation, because I think the government has made one of the most serious blunders in respect of housing; I would say more about it if this were the appropriate time to do so. This is the note I find in the document before me:
A total of 89,015 new housing units were completed in 1950, approximating the record of 1949. Since the number of starts was 92,531 (a little greater than 1949) the number under construction at the year end also showed an increase, and amounted to 60,538. This would suggest a continuing high level of completion in the first part of 1951.
I believe this could be maintained, by the exercise of a little bit of care. Certainly there is no reason why we cannot produce a great number of houses of a lower value for those in lower income brackets. The fact we do not do it is the result purely of government mismanagement.
Then, what about furnishings? Furniture is in good supply. I am told, too, that there is a good supply of floor coverings. The supply of electrical apparatus was up by 25 per cent at the end of December, 1950. What about sheet metal products? Shipments increased by 90 per cent over the previous year. Stocks, at the same time, were at the same high level.
Then, what about hardware? The situation is substantially the same as in the case of sheet metal products. What about soaps? The supply has increased markedly over the year, and inventories are again higher. What about paints? The same observation applies as in connection with soaps.
Then, what about fuel and lighting? I find there was 40 per cent more coal available for consumption in the latter part of 1950 than there was in 1949. Our oil supply seems to be adequate; we have no difficulty obtaining it. What about gasoline and gas? We seem to have plenty of it. What about manufactured gas? The supply has increased. What about natural gas? The sales increased by almost 40 per cent late in 1950.
Here is an example of the kind of thing that is happening in respect of fuels. Let us take coal. I read now from a document which came from the Canada Information Agency, of which Mr. John S. Connolley is director. This article is dated May 31, 1951, and says:
Lately the mechanical efficiencies of the oil and gas industry have been very much in the news, especially in North America. But the changes planned in the coal mining industry are just as spectacular and worthy of attention.
One of the latest mechanical devices being introduced into the soft coal industry of the United States is the continuous mining machine. It provides the nearest approach yet made to continuity of production at the coal face. The machine promises to telescope the four conventional steps

Excise Tax Act
of modern mining-cutting, drilling, blasting and loading-into one operation. Usually these steps have needed separate machines and separate crews.
The new "do-all" machine cuts and loads at the coal face in one operation and does away with the need for drilling and blasting. Demonstrations have shown that the coal industry must develop faster methods of transporting coal away from the new high-speed machines in order to allow them to operate without a pause. Where they have been tried, they have, under certain conditions, tripled the output of miners at the coal face and lowered the costs of production.
Several types of these machines have already been developed in the United States. One is a chain-cutter which rips the coal out, another chips it away, a third is a burster-type machine and others wedge out the coal or break it loose with vibrators.
Several types of conveyor systems have been evolved to work with the cutting machines. One which has been in use in West Virginia for almost a year Is reported to have moved coal from the face at the rate of 45 tons per man-shift. The usual average with other methods was about ten tons per man-shift. Another new conveyor type is the "piggy-back" machine. It literally rides piggyback on the loading machine at one end and on the first unit of the.transportation system at the other, making possible a continuous movement of coal to the surface. It can be used with the conventional loading machines or with the new continuous mining machines.
I see no indication there of any possible shortage of coal, if we chose to introduce this machinery. Then, our gasoline supply is more than five per cent higher than at the year's end.
Then, what are some of the general facts? Were retail sales during January and February, 1951, greater or less than in the same two months of 1950? They were almost 19 per cent greater. Again, were sales in grocery stores up or down? They were up by 13 per cent. Were sales in country general stores up or down? They were up by 15 per cent. In department stores they were up 16 per cent. Sales of family clothing were up 13 per cent, and sales in shoe stores were up 19 per cent. Then, motor vehicle outlets indicate that sales were up 47 per cent. What about lumber and building materials? They were up 20 per cent. What about household appliances? They were up 23 per cent.
This all indicates there is an adequate supply. True, people are buying freely, but the supply must be coming along. What other general facts can we state? Inventories on hand available for shipment-what about them? Were total inventories of goods in December of 1950 higher or lower than in December of 1949? They were 10 per cent higher. How did this apply to non-durables? It applies only slightly. How did it apply to semi-durables? It applied only to the extent of 20 per cent. How about durables? It applied to the extent of 30 per cent.

Does a general survey of major commodity groups important to the welfare of the Canadian economy indicate any serious shortage of consumer goods? The answer is No.
What about steel? Well, the steel situation seems to be somewhat beclouded. The report seems to be different, depending upon the person one talks with. However here is a press clipping which I think is worthy of note. It is dated at Ottawa, May 8, a Canadian Press dispatch and states:
Trade officials said yesterday that the steel situation in Canada is gradually moving towards stabilization.
Though the need' still is for more steel, boosted production and increased supplies from the United States had lifted some of the pressure from a critical situation that existed earlier this year, the officials said.
"At least, we can see where we are going," one authority said. "With the supplies we've got, and those we hope to get, no emergency program in Canada should suffer."
The trend towards stabilization will mean no immediate easing of current steel controls, levied mostly against the construction industry. However, as long as it continues, it would1 mean that further controls planned would not be enforced.
That indicates that our steel production is coming into good shape. Since all these things are true, and if I correctly interpret them, I think there can be no reason under the sun why we should make any further reduction in the purchasing power in the hands of the people. We are able to produce enough goods, just as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, unless we get into allout war. We are able to produce enough goods to supply comforts to the people of Canada. I maintain that all these imposts we are contemplating in this bill, virtually every one of them and particularly the increase in the sales tax, will decrease the comfort of the people. We have already cut down the practical purchasing power of a large percentage of the Canadian people to a point where it is painfully lower than it was ten years ago.
I believe this situation is very serious, Mr. Speaker. I suggest it is easy enough for a country like Canada to begin looking down, to begin to think we cannot do big things. This country of Canada is capable of tremendous achievements. All we need to do is to manage it right, have faith in ourselves and adopt sound financial and economic measures. Then, we shall not have to bring into existence such taxes as these, which we have now, in order to raise money. We can create money through the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to go into detail, but I am going to draw the attention of those who desire to read something about this matter of creating money to Hansard of April 19, 1951, pages 2195 to 2202; April 30,

1951,	pages 2519 to 2526; May 1, 1951, pages 2558 to 2563; May 22, pages 3303 to 3305, where I discussed the Guernsey island situation; May 23, pages 3314 to 3318, where I discussed the greenback situation.
I maintain that if the principles that are laid down in those pages are adopted by the government in power it is ridiculous for us to talk about having to adopt imposts such as these to raise money on which to run the country, raising the price of goods at the same time. We can only make one disastrous mistake, and in my judgment we are on the verge of making that disastrous mistake. If we go too far and break things in this country and bring on a depression while a war is in progress we shall have real trouble. That is an extremely easy thing to do. There have been three or four danger signals hung out by men who are particularly qualified to speak about these matters. There was an announcement over the air today by one eminent man to the effect that if the government went on with the control of credit there would be widespread unemployment. Let widespread unemployment appear in this country and I shall defy this government, or any three governments with no more intelligence than this one, to tell us how to get out of it. It is easy enough to break down the confidence of the people so they will go out of production and go into ruin, but it is a difficult thing to build up their confidence. The men who were in power in this country during 1931, 1932 and 1933 found that out. I urge, Mr. Speaker, that we do not adopt any more injurious methods of this kind, but that we begin to canvass the possibility of financing our needs by sound economic methods.
I am therefore, Mr. Speaker, personally unalterably opposed to the principle of this bill. I am going to oppose it with all the energy I have, and I am going to vote for the amendment.

Excise Tax Act
Motion agreed to on division, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Dion in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Duty paid value.

I want to
ask a question with respect to section 2(b)
(ii) .	I find difficulty in constructing that provision particularly by reason of the inclusion of the words "advertising, financing, servicing". I am wondering exactly how those fit into the definition of "sale price". My question has regard particularly to the wording of section 2, which amends section 79 of the act. Paragraph (b) provides:
"Sale price," for the purpose of determining the excise tax payable under this part, means the aggregate of
(ii) any amount that the purchaser is liable to pay to the vendor by reason of or in respect of the sale in addition to the amount charged as price (whether payable at the same time or some other time) including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any amount charged for, or to make provision for, advertising, financing, servicing, warranty-
My question first of all has to do with the word "servicing". If your original charge includes something for servicing I think I can understand the significance and perhaps the reasonableness of the definition, but suppose servicing is something paid for from time to time by the purchaser later, which I take it is quite possible. Will that then be included in the amount taxed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Servicing which is part of the condition of sale is included in the sale price. Later servicing, if it is a separate item, .is not included. If the hon. member will turn to the next page and the explanation for section 5 he will see that section 2 and section 5 actually define the same thing, sale price. Section 2 has relation to the excise tax and section 5 tc the sales tax. Actually the wording is the same. The cost of servicing, of warranties, of advertising if need be, if included* in the cost of the sale is part of the sale price. This is the present practice and has been continued in exactly the same form for the establishment of sale price for the purpose of levying excise tax as for the purpose of levying sales tax. The note on the right hand side of the second page under section 5 is perhaps better than the note on the first page.

In paragraph
(iii)	apparently the sale price includes the amount of excise duty paid also.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is excise duty, not excise tax. Sale price includes customs or excise duties, that is duties on liquor, for example, in

a warehouse, or a distillery. When that moves out it has paid its excise duty, and it then becomes subject to sales and excise taxes. Those latter taxes are levied on the same price; they do not pyramid, but the sales tax is levied on the cost including the customs or excise duty.
You mean the sales tax is levied on the price of the goods plus the customs or excise duty?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.
Does the excise duty apply to other articles than tobacco and liquor?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Just those two.

I come back: to the word servicing. The parliamentary assistant has told us what it means, and that it would cover a servicing charge paid subsequently from time to time. However, I do not see that this is clear from the wording; and from what has occurred already in this house tonight we want to be very clear as to the meaning of things.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As an example, most refrigerators carry one year's free servicing. That is a condition of sale, and of course that cost [DOT] to the company giving the guarantee is embedded in the cost of the refrigerator. At the end of that year the owner can enter into other servicing arrangements for the next three or four years, if need be, either with the company from which he bought the refrigerator or with another company. That is a separate thing having no relation to the sale price. The actual service given for the first year is a cost to the company providing that service and selling the refrigerator, and under this definition that cost is embedded in the sale price.

That seems very reasonable, and I do not doubt that it is so, but it does not seem to me that this wording makes clear that it is so, and I am wondering whether there should not be something to make it perfectly clear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All I can say is that this is the exact wording in the present act, and that is the policy that has been followed. There is no change in this wording, as the hon. member will see if he looks over the bill.

It is not
quite as clear as that. In tne explanatory note I read that hitherto the absence of a definition of sales price to cover the excise tax has left the basis of application of the tax uncertain. Am I not right in thinking this is supposed to introduce a clarity that has not been there previously?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is here to make it abundantly clear that the same basis is used to ascertain the sale price for both the excise tax and the sales tax. Previously, as far as the levying of the excise tax was concerned, there was no specific definition of sales price. The sale price definition used was that spelled out under the sales tax. Now under both the excise tax section and the sales tax section we are having exactly the same definition we now have in the act for sale price with regard to sales tax.
The word "financing" I presume applies to finance charges which may be collected on deferred payments. Are they added to the cost of the article before the imposition of sales tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All this, of course, is not at the consumer level; this is the manufacturer selling. If the manufacturer is selling these articles on time, then the cost of his financing is included in the cost price of the refrigerator, for example. After all, that is the only place he can put it.
Supposing the financing is done by an outside corporation. Do you charge sales tax on the finance charges in that case?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If it is done by an outside corporation, no; only if it is done by the company selling the article.
Some of these people add their finance charges and then turn around and refinance with finance companies. What happens in that case?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Once again, the purpose of this is to see that the sales price by the manufacturer to his customer is the actual selling price including the cost of the goods and the
Excise Tax Act
cost of financing and servicing. The actual object here is to prevent a manufacturer breaking up his selling price into a variety of items and saying there was so much for the actual material, so much for the cost of servicing for the next year, so much for the cost of carrying the retailer's finance charges for a year and so on, and then saying the sales tax should be levied only on the actual cost of the material. We regard the sale price as the cost at which the manufacturer sells to the retailer, including all these costs he has incurred.
Then if a manufacturer allows a discount for cash do you permit him to apply the sales tax to the net amount after the discount has been deducted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is quite right.
